utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday. Good afternoon to all the people in the courtroom, to the accused, the Defence counsel, Mr. Scott, Mr. Kruger, and their associates and their manager, and all the people helping us. Mr. Registrar, you have four IC numbers for us first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Batinic, Zdravko. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00881. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00882. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00833. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00834, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit number IC 00835. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There seems to be a virus going around, so if one of the accused doesn't feel well, of course he's authorised to leave the courtroom, if he feels the need to do so. I first have to hand down an oral decision as to the request for translation for the expert report by witness Cvikl. On the 10th of October, 2008, the Prlic Defence filed, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, an expert report written in English by Milan Cvikl. At the hearing of the 15th of October, 2008, the Prlic Defence requested the Trial Chamber to instruct and direct the Registry to have the report translated into B/C/S for the needs of the Prlic Defence. The Stojic Defence joined the motion. The Trial Chamber notes that the expert report was filed well past the date of the 31st of March, 2008, which was the initial deadline set by the Trial Chamber; that therefore the request for translation is a late one. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber notes that this report was drafted in English, one of the two working languages of the Tribunal, and that the counsel and co-counsel respectively for the Prlic and Stojic Defence have a perfect command of English. Therefore, they are in a position to convey the contents of the report to their respective clients and to receive instructions from them for them to carry out the cross-examination of Witness Cvikl, if the latter is to testify. The Trial Chamber, therefore, is of the view that the accused Prlic and Stojic do not suffer any prejudice if the Trial Chamber decides not to order the Registry Translation Service to have the expert witness report translated into B/C/S. As a result, the Trial Chamber decides that it is not for the Registry Translation Services to translate the expert report into B/C/S, but that, if need be, the Prlic Defence have to have it done. Mr. Khan, I believe you want to say something to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, Mr. President. The request to have it translated was not for our benefit. It was for the benefit of others, and it gives the impression that somehow we're shifting the burden. But we were trying to make it available to those who wished to have it. But we take the -- we accept the oral ruling as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Khan, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm grateful. And good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Your Honours, we received this morning a consolidated response by the Prosecution to the applications -- yes, Your Honours, this should be closed session. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ideally, the Prosecution would finish their cross-examination today. The Prosecution has under four hours, if failing objections we could make it, and tomorrow Mr. Karnavas could have the time he needs for redirect. I said "ideally speaking." Of course, we don't know what's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're delighted to see you again. As you know, you're coming back into this courtroom to finish the end of cross-examination and redirect. If all goes well, the Prosecutor should finish today with his cross-examination, and tomorrow Mr. Karnavas could have his redirect, so that by Wednesday you can return to your normal life. Mr. Scott, you have the floor. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, all of you. Good afternoon to counsel and all those in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Tomic. And again as others have said, welcome back. Sir, just to start with some procedural -- very quickly with some procedural matters and just so the record is clear, I assume we know what the answers are, but can we understand, sir, that since the last time you were here on the 4th of November, you have not talked to anyone about the testimony you gave last time or the testimony that you might anticipate giving today or tomorrow, you haven't spoken to anyone about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that you have not reviewed any documents or any materials of any sort in connection with preparing to testify since you were here last year [sic] on the 4th of November.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think we need to quickly review, if we can, so -- since you were here some more than ten days ago, just quickly where we were. Among other things, sir, on the 4th of November I had shown to you a document of a record of a meeting with President Tudjman on the 8th of January, 1992, which, for the record, is Exhibit P00108. Perhaps if I mention it to you, this was the meeting with President Tudjman also involving Mr. Franjo Boras and the Bosnian Serb leader, Mr. Koljevic. You might remember it. There was a part of the transcript which I did not cover at the time and entirely my oversight, and if we could look that again which I think will also serve at the same time to essentially bring us back up to speed. If I can ask you -- I think all the binders -- if we could have all the ushers -- thank you very much. In binder -- it's Exhibit 00108. I think that will be in the first binder. If I can ask you, sir, in that transcript -- and again I'll remind you that in all of this so-called presidential transcript material, the page numbers in both English and the Croatian language versions should be the same. So if I refer you to page 9, it should be page 9 in both versions. And, in fact, I will ask you, please, to go to page 9. This is -- this was Mr. Koljevic continuing to talk -- excuse me. On page 9, sir, about the second paragraph beginning on that page, it says: "Therefore, we proposed a confederal status for Bosnia at least as the first stage in which, if one views it constructively, the Croatian national community and the Serbian national community could have free confederal ties with Croatia and Serbia." If you'll then go to the next page, page 10, just continuing that same discussion, and the first paragraph on page 10 it continues: "Of course, we can speak principally about Bosnia and Herzegovina, although I would be glad if we, as Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina, could mediate a bit, offer our good services if you so desire and if that proves feasible. Likewise, in this broader Serbian and Croatian area, it seems to us - I spoke with Radovan Karadzic about this last night - we both think that this could be the beginning of an overall settlement of Serbo-Croatian relations. If we don't solve these relations, then, if I may say so, there is no end. "Then the rest in this political crisis would be far easier." And then if I could ask you, please, to go on over to page 41. And again after language intervention, that is, by Mr. Koljevic, the second paragraph under his name, Ms. Koljevic says: "First, I think that we should follow this road politically because a certain social acceptance, a climate, should be created. In Bosnia, Croats and Serbs have created a very negative climate, and if we were Bosnians and Herzegovinians, so it is a little discomfiting to say whether you are a Serb or a Croat. We have to put an end to that climate." Now, skipping to about halfway down through the next paragraph,

utterances.speaker: MR. KOLJEVIC CONTINUES
utterances.text: "We studied the map and those municipalities, and then we saw that the same thing had been done with the Croats and with the Serbs. So these enclaves, which can be established on the municipal level, they should be delimited, and then we should see what can be done with the transfer, what can be accomplished by agreement, and we should institute fair exchanges and create an agency for the civilised transfer of property and population which will be in the interest of those people. The term 'homogeneity' was, as you know, vilified in Yugoslavia. Why should it be something terrible for people to live with people who are closest to them?" And that brings us back, sir, if you go over to the top of page 42, to where we were, and that's where we read when you were here last. President Tudjman comes back into the conversation and says, in response to what was just said: "Wherever national problems so conceived emerge as they did with us, that was resolved from World War I and World War II, that was brought to a conclusion by exchanges." Now, that's the topic we were generally talking about, if you will, the demographic issues and the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina when we finished the last time you were here. I also showed to you Exhibit P08623, which you may wish to turn to. You may not have to, but just so you know what I'm referring to. That was the statement that I showed you about -- that Mr. Pogarcic had made. You may remember that. And among other things, in that interview Mr. Pogarcic said that as long as an ethnic group was not more than 10 per cent of the population, they can function as an ornament and "can even serve as proof of the will to create a multiethnic society." Now, moving forward based on that, if you look back at Mr. Pogarcic's article again, which is again P08623, one of the things that Mr. Pogarcic says in that statement, which I didn't read to you today but we looked at it the last time, he said that all three of the ethnic groups, Serbs, Muslims and Croats, during the 1991 to 1995 period "ethnically cleansed territories wherever they could." And do you agree -- I was wondering, do you agree with that statement that all three of the ethnic groups, if you will, ethnically cleansed territories wherever they could?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of ethnic demographics, isn't it true that the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership took a number of steps throughout this period 1991 to 1995 to increase the number of Croats in a desired area and to reduce the number of Muslims in that or those areas; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that in fact there were even housing projects that were established and implemented for the specific purposes of increasing the Croat population in certain areas?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were projects that were developed following the Washington and Dayton Accords, when some people decided that they would not be returning to the areas in which they were minorities. They were provided aid, in terms of building their own homes wherever they chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's turn next, then, to Exhibit P08545, which will be in the second binder. P08545. And, sir, this is a record of another meeting in the offices of President Tudjman, on this occasion dated the 27th of March of 1995. And I'd like to direct your attention, please, to page 14. Now, some parts of this relate to another topic, but rather than come back to this transcript again, I'm going to try to deal with this particular document at one time, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have a standing objection, as of last week, that anything that goes outside the four corners of the indictment, the period of the indictment, you know, that should prohibit the Prosecution from going into those areas. Again, I just want to make sure that I'm very, very clear, because I think the Prosecution is politicising this trial and now we're prosecuting the implementation of the Dayton Accords. And if that is the case, then I do think that we need to desperately have a hearing about this to determine whether we should file any appropriate motions as a result of the expanding of the indictment with the acquiescence of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had this discussion last week. The Prosecution explained very extensively what their position was. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just so the record is clear in response -- I appreciate the Court's ruling, but just so the record is clear, in case it may come up again: Since the last time Mr. Tomic was here -- I went through his testimony to date, and I have 14 pages of excerpts of his direct examination referring to the Washington Agreement and Dayton, 14 pages of transcript excerpts, so Mr. Karnavas went into these topics extensively, if there's any doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you look on page 14, toward the bottom, where there is a passage attributed to Mr. Prlic, it says: "Mr. President, not to burden you with too many facts, and the president of the party here has here presented 56 various facts, I think the main question today is one of overall political relations. I will just say a couple of sentences about that at the end. Since I am the prime minister and deputy prime minister who ruled in the Federation, in Sarajevo, just a couple of words about it so that we may have a rounded picture of the current situation. At this moment, those free areas of the Federation function as two state entities and as two completely separate states within its internal structure. They are the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, these are territories controlled by the Republic of BH Army." Excuse me: "Therefore, these are territories controlled by the Republic of BH Army. Why do I say two states? According to all the constituent elements, these are two completely different states. For instance," and this is something we talked about extensively when you were here before, "the usual customs procedure is undertaken when goods from HB, Herceg-Bosna, enter that region and is the same procedure when goods arrive from Germany, Austria or Canada. They are two completely separate entities." Now, skipping down toward the end of that full paragraph, Mr. Prlic continues --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that he be allowed to read the entire passage. If he's going to cherry-pick from this, I would expect that he allow at least the entire passage of what Mr. Prlic is saying. This is proper procedure, and it should be transferred -- the burden should not be transferred on redirect, especially when you are granting more time to them and you are not granting more time to me within the overall time frame that you have allotted me. This is fundamentally unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, to respond, Your Honour, number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, this practice -- and Mr. Karnavas -- the Chamber well knows by now this is something Mr. Karnavas says every time, and we have the same discussion every time. We can't read the entire documents, and Mr. Karnavas, in his cross -- in his direct examination, excuse me, with this witness, with the witness last week, did exactly the same thing. He takes a document and he puts to the witness those parts which he wants to put to the witness. And then he turns around and says the Prosecution should not be allowed to do the same thing. Now, that's just not the case, and it's not improper procedure, and there is no issue here about the time given to Mr. Karnavas. The Chamber's indicated already that it apparently intends to be very liberal with the amount of redirect given to Mr. Karnavas, so I don't think there's an issue about that at all. But in any event, in any event, the procedure that I follow is completely the proper one and the accepted practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not a matter -- Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, one moment, please, one moment. The Trial Chamber dismissed your objection. Through this witness, it is important for the Trial Chamber to know how he perceived what Mr. Prlic may have said. So rather than waste time on knowing how the question was put, whether it merits an objection, I think it's better for everybody to focus on the very text. That is what matters. And it is in the very interests of Dr. Prlic. He said something, but the witness may as well confirm or deny or give the specification. You, in your redirect, you will have the opportunity to go back to the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the text speaks for itself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you raised an objection. The other party answered. The Chamber has told you that it has taken a decision, and that's it. We are not going on to have these endless discussions. Last Thursday morning was really an abyss of loss of time. That's it. There's a decision, Mr. Karnavas, and please, Mr. Scott, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I will continue to object as long as the Trial Chamber allows the Prosecution to take text out of context. He should be allowed to look at the entire text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have made that point, and you can object every time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, where I left off, and if you go to the end of that paragraph, Mr. Prlic continues: "They still do not have salaries, and salaries, yes or no, are the foremost political issue here, and they will not be able to enter that process. This will be extremely important later when we talk about the Federation, with the problem being exceptionally complex in a technical sense, I believe viewed statically, it cannot be resolved at all. Mr. President, as far as the Federation is concerned, nothing has been done so far in the functional sense. Not a single function of the Federation has been developed." And I just note for you, sir, and the courtroom, this is March 1995. This is a year after the signing of the Washington Agreement: "Not a single function of the Federation has been developed. Therefore, these are all just a few psychological effects. It exists or it does not exist. However, not a single function of the Federation has been established, developed, or implemented. Because of this, officials in the Federation normally have found themselves in the situation where their authority and posts are being jeopardised, and that process is the way it is. They assess that within this time frame, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna would grow stronger, contrary to their primary aim. They have two primary aims at this moment. The first is to topple the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the other is to assure access to the sea. So these are the two basic aims." Can you confirm, sir, that by November -- excuse me, by March of 1995, based on your involvement in these issues and the various senior positions that you held at the time that you've described to the Judges, that in fact by March 1995, essentially nothing substantial had been done to establish the Federation, it was not functioning?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before during my evidence, when the Croatian representatives arrived in Sarajevo, the implementation of the Washington Agreement began, as well as the attempt to build up the Federation. Likewise, as I've mentioned, we drew up analyses to see how the financial system would be functioning in BH-controlled territory and HVO-controlled territory. I, as the finance minister of the Republic and the Federation, tabled a proposal to the government of package measures that were to be adopted. My own ministry prepared a total of 26 regulations covering that area, such as customs, taxes, budgetary law and so on and so forth. However, there was obstruction --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the interruption. It was an open-ended question. He's entitled. He said nothing was developed. He didn't say by whom. Now that he doesn't like the answer, because now he's realising that it was the Muslim authorities of Sarajevo that refused -- that refused to implement the Washington Accord. They totally did not want a federation to exist. What they wanted was a unitary state, and that's what they were trying to do. That's what the witness is trying to explain and I object to the interruption. We can't have it both ways, we can't have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Mr. Witness, please proceed, please complete, because you were discussing the 26 regulations, you will explain, and the Prosecutor interrupted you. So please complete what you were going to say, why the 26 regulations did not see the light of day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those regulations were passed, but the basic question was not resolved about the establishment of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; what army, what about the police? According to the Washington Agreement, the police was set up at the cantonal level, but we cannot now finance the budget of the state, and in accordance with the Washington Agreement, first a law on police had to be passed, a law on the army, the laws regulating the beneficiaries of the budget, and pressure was exerted in this sense. And we talked about the media reports in an effort to create the impression that Croats were opposed to the implementation of the Washington Agreement. However, no regulations defining this area that I was talking about, the budget, the expenditures, the institutions of the Federation, was passed [as interpreted], because the Bosniak side was not interested in establishing the Federation before it knew what would happen with the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was its only goal. And this was why pressure was exerted for the funds to be channeled into the budget of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But where were they supposed to be spent? And this was the basic reason why these regulations were not implemented. Later on, when we insisted for the establishment of the Federation for -- for the governments of the Federation and the Republic to be divided, the process was able to move on. Let me give you an example. In accordance with the Washington Agreement, it was envisaged that there would be the Central Bank of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the currency, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to have its own currency. At no stage did the Bosniak colleagues want to pass the law on the Central Bank of the Federation, but they said, well, there is the National Bank of the State of the Republic of Herzegovina and we have the BH dinar. But we focused on the implementation of the Federation, and we insisted that the law on the Central Bank of the Federation be passed. Of course, this document never saw the light of day, and that is one of the reasons why there was this continuous obstruction and this creating of the atmosphere of the impression that Croats were trying to obstruct it. I'm talking about people who came to Sarajevo fully intending to implement the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One minor correction. On page 16, line 15, the gentleman indicated was not passed. As it reflects now in the transcript, it says "was passed." It should say "was not passed." Page 16, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Coming back to that part of the transcript that more directly relates to the issue that we were on, in terms of demographics and some of the ethnic issues, if I can ask you to go to page 18 of the record, and this continues to be Mr. Prlic speaking, and the first paragraph starting at page 18, Mr. Prlic says: "As regards the conference, one speaks of the emotional and basic ties with Herceg-Bosna. That is why this is important, I tell you, most Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina do not feel emotional towards BH, our integral group here, ourselves, do not feel it is our state. I know this. I was at the talks on Thursday and Friday, on the other side of the table. Therefore, that is the only significant and emotional charge and we must bear it in mind at all times. That is why I believe that what we say politically, confederation as the precondition of this," and that's something we're going to hopefully get to today, as has been mentioned to the Judges, the topic of the confederation, and Mr. Prlic says: "That is why I believe that what we say politically, confederation as the precondition of this, is that we must make it operational through the appropriate decisions and test, let us say, the will of the Muslims." Then continuing at the bottom of that page, the last line on page 18: "And the third issue, Mr. Markovic, as the projects we have mentioned to you, it is the construction of a thousand individual housing units in the areas of Capljina, Dubrava, Stolac, and the southern part of Mostar which we believe will strengthen the Croatian spine in that exceptionally important area." And that brings me back, sir, to the question we were a few moments ago. Wasn't that specifically being done to increase the Croatian population and demographics in those areas, as a way of maintaining Croatian control in those areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a pragmatic response to the situation and the number of refugees in those areas, refugees who lived in other people's apartments and houses, and they had to leave those houses and apartments. And the alternative solution that was offered to them was for houses to be built for them there, because they did not want to go back to those places for the most part in Central Bosnia from where they had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that the HVO authorities and many Croats of Herzegovina were not eager to live again with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot generalise. In the areas where fighting was fierce and where there were victims in people's families, the wounds were still fresh and it was difficult to act politically to make the people go back to their -- to the places where they used to live immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was a great deal of concern among the Herceg-Bosna leadership, was there not, about Muslims coming back or returning to the so-called Croat areas?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims lived in Croatian areas until the war broke out between Croats and Muslims. So they were there, and the basic problem was the relationship of the victims, the people who suffered, and this was the general problem that prevented the return of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, this issue that is important, we see that Mr. Prlic intervenes before Mr. Tudjman, and the date is after the Washington Accords. The situation that you experienced, because you were minister of the Federation, the ethnic groups, the Serbs, the Muslims and the Croats, owing to the BiH offensive, were there areas taken by the Muslim armed forces where the Croats were to remain and did not allow the return of the Croats? Do you have knowledge of any situation where theoretically, within the framework of the Washington Accords, there were to be significant changes, by way of an example, if you know any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we constantly received information about the attacks on the returnees in Central Bosnia, parts of Jablanica. Those are people who were there as refugees, Muslims. That was their reaction. So this was an atmosphere where the blood was still boiling in people's veins after the conflicts that had taken place. So we're talking about those areas where Croats were supposed to return, in particular in Central Bosnia around Travnik, where we would receive information to that effect. And I mentioned Jablanica, Doljani, those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. So you cite the case of Jablanica. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you mentioned the -- if you will, the Muslims' reaction to some of the returns in Central Bosnia. But, sir, it was the same on the Croat side concerning so-called Muslim returns, wasn't it? There were many people, including people, I put it to you, in the HVO leadership who were opposed to the Muslims either staying or coming back to these so-called Croat areas; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already noted that the situation was so fresh in people's memories, and there was mutual situation of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go to Exhibit P08848, which will be in the second of the large binders. P08848. If I can direct your attention to page 3 of this record of a meeting involving, among others, Mr. Prlic and Mr. Tudjman. Mr. Prlic, on page 3: "With regards to the return of people, Central Bosnia, Sarajevo, Posavina and that part, he asked me whether all of that would be successful. I gave him that book. He said, 'We should meet again many times before the perfect peace is restored.'" Skipping to the next paragraph, he says: "He asked me what I thought about that. I told him that the Croats did not want to return to the areas with the majority of the Muslim population." Next page: "I gave him my example. I did not want to bring my daughters to the predominantly Muslim town, because I am afraid that they might get married to the Muslim guys. This is how I look at it, as a parent." Now, that's what Mr. Prlic said, and isn't that a commonly-held view among the Croats of Herzegovina around this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is 1998. What does this have to do with the indictment? You know, I'm objecting on the grounds of relevance. I would like to hear what the relevance is. Why is this relevant to the indictment? We keep talking about Croats. Now we're vilifying all of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He talks about, you know, the Herceg-Bosna leadership. Who are the leaderships? What is the relevance of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, among other things, Your Honour, it goes to Mr. Prlic's state of mind and attitudes in this regard, number 1. Number 2, the witness just said a few moments ago, and I thought it was quite interesting and actually quite connected, because he was attributing these emotions to the fresh wounds, if you will, the fresh wounds after the 1993-1994 war. Well, we can see here that apparently those feelings remained the same even by 1998, some years after these fresh wounds, which undoubtedly were significant, but it's entirely relevant and goes directly to the witness's testimony, Your Honour. Sir, that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I get a ruling, please? May I get a ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the view of the Chamber, it is relevant and fully acceptable, all the more so since Mr. Prlic continues indicating that, "I think that the visit of the Pope here is important." So this also seems to be linked to the Pope's visit. Witness, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, aware of what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the visit of the Pope that was likely to improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was the president of the state committee for the Pope's visit to Sarajevo, and I knew about those activities. And his arrival was supposed to be a political message, a message of support to the Croats to stay in Bosnia, to remain there, because Croats, as the smallest ethnic community, after all that they'd been through, felt some fear that they would not be able to remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a constituent people in the areas where Muslims were in the majority. They did not -- didn't have schools in Croatian, and children were not coming back, for the most part. People who were going back were the elderly, who just went there to guard the property. So I think that the lobbying for the visit of the Pope was an important effort -- an important project for the people in -- for the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, I come back to the original question some minutes ago before the objection from Mr. Karnavas. The view expressed by Mr. Prlic, when he said, "I told him that the Croats did not want to return to the areas with a majority Muslim population, I did not want to bring my daughters to the predominantly Muslim town," that was a view held not only by Mr. Prlic, but by a number of people in the HVO Herceg-Bosna leadership even by 1998; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Prlic here expressed the fears of many people, many Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when he said that. I know that this is not his view, as far as his family is concerned, because as far as I know, his brother was married twice, both of his wives were Muslims, so family-wise there are no problems there. But there was this fear that existed, and this was a way to convey those concerns. It was just an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was -- if you can go to page 8 of the same document, please. President Tudjman, in this conversation, Mr. Prlic at one point says: "My dear Jadranko," referring to him by first name: "My dear Jadranko, Zubak is one line, you are another, those down there are third one, and that's the problem." And Mr. Jadranko Prlic says: "Mr. President, I do not belong to any line. I have listened to your advice." And just repeating that at the end of that paragraph he says: "I do not belong to any line. I have been implementing what you were telling me all the time." In your close association with Mr. Prlic through this time, and learned when you were here before that you were I think it fair to say close friends and close professional associates, if I can say "professional," in government, et cetera, you were very close to Mr. Prlic. And does this not accurately state, indeed, his actions and views at the time, that this was he followed what President Tudjman told him to do? Or to quote his own words: "I have been implementing what you were telling me all the time"?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic is pragmatic by nature, very much so, and in his relations with President Tudjman, that was the stance that he took in order to get the information, because all the negotiations that were going on and all the information that came in came in, for the most part, through Zagreb, so in this context I think that his relationship with President Tudjman was a correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's something that is lacking for us Judges, at least as far as I'm concerned. It seems that this conversation between Tudjman and Prlic is linked to the departure of Zubak. What happened? What happened with Zubak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zubak founded a new party. He left the HDZ and founded a new party. That was called "The New Croatian Initiative."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why did he leave the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout this time, the HDZ functioned as a movement of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was not actually set up as a party, if you look at the membership, if you look at how it functioned. I gave you my example, where I became a member of the Presidency of the party ex officio, although I never actually became a member of that party. And then, at a later stage, when there was a period of peace, when Bosnia and Herzegovina was going through a reconstruction, of course there were different views and visions as to how things should go on from there, expounded by various people. And Zubak was the first to actually leave the HDZ and to find a new party. Mr. Prlic did the same thing at a later date, and there were others that followed. Be that as it may, new parties were created in Bosnia and Herzegovina, new Croat parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic created what, what party? What party did he create?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic founded a party that was called "The European Movement," something like that, and it was a multiethnic party. It was not a Croat ethnic party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And given Mr. Zubak created his party, Mr. -- his party, what did Mr. Tudjman have to say to that? I mean, did he see all this powerlessly? I mean, how did he react to all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't give you an answer to that question, because I really don't know how he saw that, but I do know that, in effect, every new party weakened the Croat chances in Bosnia and Herzegovina because votes were dispersed, and Croats, as a small community, were still bound to the HDZ as the first party that was set up. Two years ago, a new party, the largest so far, was founded. This party is called "The HDZ 1990." So it's the same name with the addition of "1990." At the local elections that were held recently, its results were much worse than the original HDZ's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can turn next on this same topic, continuing on to Exhibit P08489. P08489, which will be in the second binder. This is a further record of a meeting involving President Tudjman and others on the 24th of November, 1995, actually quite close in time to one of the earlier records we looked at. If I can direct your attention, please, to page 6, which again will pick up with Mr. Prlic talking. Page 6, a few lines down in the first paragraph on that page, Mr. Prlic says: "In that connection, our basic demand to the Muslim side has a particular gravity, so we would ask you to try to resolve it with Mr. Izetbegovic. It's about addressing the question of demarcating the borders between the 'velezupe,' or cantons as we now call them, within the framework of the Federation. You know what our interest is in that respect. Under the Vienna agreement, these newly liberated areas are not included in the Federation territory, because in any case that process has to be met. It's vital also because of the next conclusion, and it's about the return of refugees and displaced persons, where we find ourselves, whether we like it or not, in a defensive position, bearing in mind that the Muslims are staying, that the Muslims don't have any other homelands to fall back on, and even at the price of far lower standards of living, they will stay and fill up our areas. That's not the case with the Croats, and in accordance with our national priorities we must ensure that when it comes to demarcation, we safeguard those areas in which - I wish to say this perfectly openly - we are keen to have a majority Croatian population." Then continuing over to the top of page 9, please, and Mr. Prlic continues on this topic, the top of page 9, please. Mr. Prlic says: "And the third aspect is support in the demographic sense. We discussed that at Dayton, too, the minister of foreign affairs and ourselves, and we must secure funds for Drvar, either on a credit basis or some other way, we are securing these areas for Croatian families to live there and be there. We have to secure funds for the families who tomorrow should be living in Ivanjica, between Dubrovnik and Trebinje, in that belt that belongs to the Federation. But there won't be any Croatian people, regardless of what the borders are, we won't be able to fully realise the interests that were the reason in the first place why we ended up drawing these borders in this part of the territory, regardless of all the arrangements that are mentioned, that we anticipated over a long, probably quite a long time." And you'll go then on the topic to page 14, bottom of page 14 where Mr. Bender comes into the conversation, and I will ask you, sir, a couple of questions about this when I put these passages to you. Bender says at the end of that paragraph above "president," he says: "I would like to ask for a concretisation of the national programme of protecting marginal territories, in addition to Dubrovnik, through Num and so on, to Central Bosnia, because if we don't concretise this, I'm afraid that the Croats will drain out from these areas and then we don't need either the Federation or Bosnia and Herzegovina. I hope that with plentiful help from the Republic of Croatia, we'll perform our task to the satisfaction of Croats." Sir, isn't it correct that throughout this time period, this continued to be a major concern of the Herceg-Bosna and HVO leadership, and that was the issue of the demographics in so-called Herceg-Bosna, and there was a concern about the loss of Croat population and an increase in Muslim population; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not in reference to that. This is the period after the Federation had been defined as a number of cantons. The Drvar area, after the combat operations in the area, remained undefined. Did it belong to the Federation or not? How would that area be organised? And this was the question. A large number of refugees, Croat refugees, had arrived in Drvar to settle there. Aid became necessary in order to enable those people to live there. We needed funds to build accommodation for them. We needed a school system to be up and running. A modicum of economy, so to speak. There was a lot of forestry there, timber processing and so on and so forth. This is not about Herceg-Bosna. This is the situation in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina following the operations during which these areas became part of the Federation. But it had not been defined yet which canton they would fall under.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's continue on this same record and see what President Tudjman says on this topic. If I can direct your attention to page 30. Page 30, please, and it picks up at the second line of the page, President Tudjman talking: "Yes, they have preserved a complete Bosnia, but one where, on the demarcation line there'll be created four kilometres. But you interpret what the Croatian people got. So the Croatian people also got territories that they didn't have, so Grahovo, not just Kupres, but Grahovo, Glamoc, Drvar and Jajce, territories, then, that are of strategic interest for the Croatian state. And it's clear that here we're to try, like down there at Stolac, to try through settling people there, you'll create," and he goes and talks about "Mr. Susak has already told you about a decision to put certain military unit in an area to cover these things and secure things for the future." The next paragraph, Mr. Tudjman goes on to say: "Don't lose confidence. Gentlemen, we've succeeded. We've succeeded in getting not just Herceg-Bosna, which is what we had, what we've got - we can say that among ourselves - half of Bosnia, if we're good at governing, if we govern cleverly." Going to the top of page 31 , President Tudjman continuing on, first paragraph on that page: "And, of course, in the Federation again, and on the basis of past experience, you have to demand that every Croatian municipality holds out and is autonomous, self-governing, or in places where Croats are scattered around, in places where they can't hold out or don't want to, get them to move to these territories that we're interested in so that in every respect, and in respect of the population itself, they take on a Croatian character." Sir, I put my question -- the same question I put to you a few moments ago, after seeing what President Tudjman says. It was a continuing demographic policy of President Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna leadership to work the demographics in such a way and to move population in such a way as to maintain Croatian control in certain desired areas; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must go back to the Constitution of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The cantons were in charge of education, the school system, the media, and so on and so forth, a number of other areas as well. This is about Drvar and Bosanska Grahovo, about these two areas. They are here becoming part of a canton that has a Croat ethnic majority, the so-called Livno canton. Within the canton, these people had their own schools with teaching in the Croatian language. They had their own media and such like. It wasn't the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's not just about Livno. It talks about Kupres, Jajce, Central Bosnia. You can't limit what President Tudjman has said to those particular areas you just mentioned. In fact, Tudjman says, "We've succeeded in not just getting Herceg-Bosna, but half of Bosnia if we govern smartly"; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this was an expression of support to the Croatian leadership, telling them to join in the effort to build Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was also a message saying that a solution could be found. I'm talking about a canton that was predominantly Croat and also a canton that had parity with the other towns in it. The schooling was cantonal level at the time, education was, and this was one of the important factors in terms of having people return to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of your testimony when you were here previously, you made a number of references or comments about the Tuzla municipality. Just one question on that, I believe. Just to be clear, during the period April 1992 to April 1994, April 1992 to April 1994, were you ever in Tuzla municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just not on Tuzla, but if I can just expand that and ask you the same question, for example, about Zenica. Were you ever in Zenica during the period April 1992 to April 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was passing through in 1992, October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that the only time that you were passing through or in Zenica during that two-year period?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about money that was flowing from the Croatian Ministry of Defence to Croatia, and we saw some of that documentation. And you made reference in that part of your testimony that, to your knowledge or in your view, this money was coming from the contributions from the Croatian Diaspora. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to put to you -- I'm putting to you now that unless you've seen or unless you've been personally involved in some sort of a very detailed and exhaustive accounting of all that money, you have no way of saying, do you, that all the money that was flowing through the Ministry of Defence came from diaspora contributions?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had received information from Mr. Martinovic, and he was one of the signatories of those accounts. It was based on that that I said that the money had arrived in these accounts, and these accounts were opened in banks outside Croatia. The implementation then went through the Defence ministry or through a number of other channels that Mr. Martinovic or Mr. Susak, as the signatories of those accounts, made sure were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat my question to you. Sir, there's no way that you can tell these Judges, under oath, that all the money that went to Herceg-Bosna or the HVO through the Croatian Ministry of Defence came from diaspora contributions, can you? You simply have no way of telling the Judges that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how I learned this. I wasn't keeping track of those accounts, and I wasn't the one doing the accounting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with Mr. Prlic and the positions he held, and you'll recall that the last time you were here you -- we looked at one of his business cards, and in fact he had a cellphone number and a telephone number and a fax number, and on that business card he described himself as the president of the Croatian -- excuse me, the president of the HVO HZ-HB; is that correct? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that in your experience, and working closely with Mr. Prlic, when he met people, when he met international officials, for example, I suppose he did not introduce himself as the convener of meetings, did he?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did he introduce you, "Hi, President so-and-so. I'm Jadranko Prlic, I'm the convener of meetings"?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I suppose at these meetings he never introduced himself as, quote, "the signer of documents."

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this line of questioning. We've heard witnesses over and over again talk about what the function was of the president of the -- of an executive authority, be it at a municipal level or at this level. I find these questions offensive, and I think that I would expect that the Trial Chamber would find them equally offensive at this point, three years into this trial. I think that this is the better time -- there are better ways to use up his time that the Trial Chamber has been so generous in giving him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Your Honour, my questions are entirely serious. Representations have been made about what powers and authorities Mr. Prlic had, and I think it's appropriate to know how did he hold himself out to the world. And I suspect, as I'm putting the questions to the witness, he didn't introduce himself as, "I convene meetings." My question is entirely serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear of Mr. Prlic explain himself or his position to international officials or others, that his position in Herceg-Bosna was, quote, "to sign documents"?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic was the president of the HVO HZ-HB, and that is precisely how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you come to know that throughout this period of 1992 to 1994, that Mr. Prlic, among other things, had a number of ongoing dealings with the Serb -- the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that there was permanent contact. I know that some information would occasionally arrive, but I knew of no permanent, ongoing contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure where the word "permanent" came from. It wasn't in my question. My question was: Did you become aware that from time to time, perhaps increasing over time, Mr. Prlic had dealings and negotiations with the Bosnian Serb authorities? And I take it the answer is, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At a later stage, there were contacts, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go to Exhibit P10718, which will be in the third binder. P10718. And I'm told that the translations for those who might want to look in the B/C/S, that those translations were distributed today that we've been able to obtain since the last time. But, in any event, P10718. Sir, this is a BBC article dated the 14th of June, 1993. It refers to Mr. Prlic being involved in negotiating for prisoner exchange with the Serb authorities. About halfway -- well, not quite halfway down the page, Mr. Prlic is said to have said he expresses his gratitude on behalf of the Croatian side to the people of the Serbian Republic for the help they have extended the Croatian civilians and fighters who had to leave the Travnik area due to the attack by the Muslim army. And then in the next paragraph after the reporter or interviewer speaks, he talks about arranging an exchange of prisoners on an all-for-all basis. Can you remind the Judges what it meant, in terms of when you negotiated a prisoner exchange, what "all-for-all" meant, and that was in contrast to what?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly an expert on exchanges, but I think "all-for-all" means all prisoners on one side were exchanged for all prisoners on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it regardless of the numbers on each side. So even though it might be -- one might be turning over 10 and the other side might be turning over 50, but rather than a one-for-one, that's the purpose of saying "all-for-all"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in this same article, it's not only actually Mr. Prlic, but it makes reference to Mr. Petkovic's involvement in these matters. And if you go down toward the bottom of the document, Mr. Petkovic is indicated -- is reported here as talking about these -- some people that have been taken prisoner, apparently. He says: "After their detainment, a different treatment would not be in accordance with what you have said. Therefore, they are civilians in my eyes. They are in uniform. I hope they will be treated as civilians and that they will be returned to us." Did you have any knowledge of that area around this time, that in June 1993 -- about any Croat soldiers who had come into the custody, if you will, of the Serbs around that time, and the issue of how they should be treated?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were Croats from Kupres who had been taken prisoner. There was a lot of pressure being exerted by the public, pushing for their release. Some of them were listed as missing, as a matter of fact. There was a very powerful association of parents and families that kept exerting pressure, sending letters, making public statements, in a bid to find their missing relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this same topic, would you go, please, next to P10717, which should be close by, the document immediately preceding the exhibit, I believe. This is another BBC article dated the 26th of June, 1993, referring to the topic of prisoner exchanges and again discussing Mr. Prlic's involvement. In the third paragraph of this document, it says that apparently the Croat side had refused to release even the 90 Serbs brought to the exchange from Livno, in Western Herzegovina. Do you have any knowledge as to why the Croats on this occasion refused to release the 90 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, it refers to 500 Serbs who had been released in the -- from the area of Tomislavgrad in October of 1992. Do you know anything about the release of those Serbs in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, that throughout this time period, Mr. Prlic, as president of the HVO HZ-HB, was engaged in prisoner exchange negotiations with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Prlic had contacts with the Serbs. It was about making sure those people received assistance, and this was probably done under pressure from the families who were looking for their relatives, all them wanting to get their relatives released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to next turn, please, to P10711. That should also be close by, P10711, another BBC-reported article on the 3rd of September, 1993, concerning talks between Mr. Prlic and the Bosnian Serb authorities on a number of topics, including freedom of movement, passage of convoys. It's in binder number 3, but it should be -- it should have been close by to the 10711. My particular question about that, other than the -- you don't have it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we have the usher's assistance, please. Binder 3, 10711. Okay. I'm told, Your Honour, that the documents the witness would have been looking would probably have been loose today, and that may be the basis of the confusion. Sir, if you could either find it, or if I could ask you to assist us, please, by looking at the screen in front of you. You'll see the same document. In the interests of time, sir, I really just have one particular question about the document. In the -- toward the bottom of the page, the last paragraph that is attributed to Mr. Prlic, you'll see Mr. Prlic's name in brackets, and toward the end of that paragraph he says: "The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna wants its neighbours in the territory of former Bosnia-Herzegovina be people open to cooperation and negotiations to ease tensions." And my question to you, sir: Was it common for the HVO and Herceg-Bosna leadership around this time in September of 1993 to refer to Bosnia-Herzegovina as the former Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't being referred to as the former, in the sense of no longer being there. The reference was to the previous Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had not been agreed, in a manner of speaking upon, and which was not the expression of the will of all its inhabitants, and that's why the term "former" was used here; not in the sense of a country no longer being around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What had not been agreed, according to the will of all its inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the changes that ensued in terms of government, in terms of the Presidency, in terms of Parliament, all these were unilateral changes made by Sarajevo, and that is what the term "former" refers to. It doesn't suggest that this is a country that is no longer there. It means that this is a state that was developed and set up and established, but not all of the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina were really involved in this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it says here -- there's no reference to the government. It says -- it's referring to territory. The territory had not changed, had it, or had it? Is your position that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had changed by 30 September 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We're talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, we're talking about a state which is within its Avnoj borders. However, colloquially, the term "former" was used, in the sense of the former authorities, a state that was not established since its establishment. This is not about new territory. This is always about Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it is former, former meaning one still seeks a structure that would suit all of its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's what you say now, but I will leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the commentary, Your Honour. You know, he can just move on with the questions. He's not here to provide commentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To hear Mr. Karnavas say that, Your Honour, is truly astounding, given the amount of running commentary that he provides on a regular basis, but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've got two minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to go next to P10709, sir. It should still be in the third binder, if you have that, 10709. Sir, this is a BBC article dated the 5th of October, 1993, again talking about certain meetings between Mr. Prlic and the Bosnian Serb authorities. It refers to a two-day visit to Banja Luka. Mr. Prlic, among other things, states that the Serbs in this area had never been at war. And in the third paragraph of that document: "... as the frontlines were frozen and the ceasefire was in force in all theaters of war." Can you confirm to the Judges, please, that as of October of 1993, there was no active large-scale fighting between the Croats and Serbs in the area of Herzegovina, was there?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't know. You can't -- you have no basis at all? You can't tell the Judges about the general state of affairs during that time between the Serb -- Bosnian Serb armed forces and Croat armed forces? Sir, isn't it correct -- let me put just it to you this way, then. Isn't it correct, sir, that for many months around this time, in fact, there had not been any significant armed conflict between Serbs and Croats in most of the areas of Herzegovina or Central Bosnia; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to raise an objection. Given the question, I think my learned friend is misleading the witness. The first time around, the way my learned friend phrased it, it was about Prlic, among other things, saying that the Serbs in this area, meaning Banja Luka, that the Serbs -- it should obviously read "Serbs and Croats" - the Serbs and Croats in this area were never fighting, and then it goes on. If it goes like that, then this is about Banja Luka. And then the questions move on to Central Bosnia, Herzegovina, and so on and so forth. We had many separate wars in Bosnia, and we all know this is a notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, was it a general question or did it have to do only with Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was a general question, Your Honour. I introduced --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I introduced the topic by simply referring to the first paragraph, but I believe by the time we get to the third paragraph, we are speaking more generally. And that was my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Witness, can you answer the question, this general question? As the Prosecutor put it, in that period there was no major conflict or fighting between the Croats and the Serbs. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not privy to any detail, where was this and so on and so forth. I really can't recall. As for this document, it's about the Banja Luka area. There were a large number of Croats living there. My family -- rather, my father hailed from Banja Luka. His family lived there. And there was no fighting, in the sense of a war being waged there. I think it was in reference to that particular segment. I don't know about the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina or anything sporadic going on elsewhere. It wasn't my place to monitor such developments. But, again, right now I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we resume with the testimony, let me give a short oral ruling regarding the request made orally by accused Prlic for an IC number to be given to a written filing by the Prosecution in relation to time. During the hearing of 13th November 2008, accused Prlic asked the Trial Chamber to give an IC number to a written submission by the Prosecution distributed during the hearing of 11 November in support of his request for additional time for cross-examination of Witness Neven Tomic. This written submission contains a comparison of the total time used by the Defence teams in order to examine and cross-examine Witnesses Neven Tomic, E.A. and Zoran Perkovic, on one hand, and the overall time used by the Prosecution for the cross-examination of those witnesses. After deliberation, the Trial Chamber dismissed -- decided to dismiss this request, because IC numbers are only given to evidence discussed and tendered into evidence through a witness. The filing in question does not belong to either category. Therefore, it cannot be given an IC number. Very well. Let's have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While the witness is coming, Your Honour, in light of your ruling, I did file a motion for certification. At this time, I make an oral request that that be part of -- that that be attached as an exhibit to the motion for certification. And I can file an amended version to that, if that would assist. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, we were on and still are on Exhibit P10709, the 5 October 1993 article. There are still several aspects of that I would like to talk to you about. We were talking about whether there had been conflict around this time between the Croats and Serbs, but perhaps we can come back to that in a few minutes. But also in that same -- the last paragraph that we were talking about before, the one that I referred you to that says: "As the frontlines were frozen ...," it then goes on to say and attributes to Mr. Prlic a statement about the economic cooperation between the two states, referring to the Serbian Republic, that is, the Republic of Srpska, and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Was it your experience around this time -- well, let me ask you, Mr. Tomic, is that the terminology you used in the fall of 1993, to refer to Herceg-Bosna as a state and the RS as a state?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No state prerogatives were used in the Herceg-Bosna nomenclature, and this is just a journalistic description.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, going to the last paragraph of this very same article, it says that Mr. Prlic said: "... Now the Republic has all the features and powers of a state." Do you disagree with Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand what you're referring to. What section?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The last paragraph, if you will, of the same article that we've been looking at for the last few minutes: "Speaking about the development of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Prlic said that now it was a republic with all the features and powers of a state." Now, do you agree with that or do you disagree with Mr. Jadranko Prlic's assessment?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot say that it had the characteristics of a state. At no time did Herceg-Bosna have this element.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the preceding paragraph, the statement is attributed to

utterances.speaker: MR. PRLIC THAT SAYS
utterances.text: "As we were not --" and he's referring, obviously, to the -- well, from the context of this article, to the Serbs, and he says: "'As we were not able to live together, we should continue to live as neighbours,' Prlic said." I put it to you, sir, that statement by Mr. Prlic sounds amazingly similar to the statement by Mr. Koljevic in the presidential record we looked at earlier. "We can live together, but not on top of each other." That was also Mr. Prlic's view, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what was said here. I know, from my contacts with Mr. Prlic, what his thoughts were on this matter, so this is not in the context of what Mr. Koljevic was saying. This was about a visit to Banja Luka and the efforts to help the Croats who remained in Banja Luka, the costs of medical treatment and various other problems that they encountered. So this part is given from the point of view of the journalist. He's the one describing the situation. But knowing what Mr. Prlic's positions were, what his thoughts were on this matter, to me this is contradictory to what his thoughts were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've said something similar to that a number of times now this afternoon, and I want to come at it this way: I put it to you, sir, are you suggesting that with a given audience on a given day, Mr. Prlic would say one thing and on a different day Mr. Prlic would say something different?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. Is the Prosecutor now claiming that these are his actual words and that the journalist accurately described what was said, if indeed anything was said? We don't have a tape-recording, we have nothing to verify this. I object to the way the question is formed. Now, if he wishes to rephrase it and to say that Dr. Prlic would say one thing on one occasion and another thing on another occasion, that's fine. But to now claim that these are his held positions, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, two responses, Your Honour. Number 1, there's no reason, at face value, not to take the article at face value. We simply cannot assume that it is not correct, number 1. Number 2, number 2, I'm happy to put the question as suggested by Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your experience, and again as a close friend and colleague of Dr. Prlic, is it your experience that depending on the circumstances and depending on the audience, Mr. Prlic might say one thing on one day and something completely different to a different audience under a different circumstance on another day?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say once again I know his views of those issues, and in this text, this is a Tanjug text that is carried by the BBC. It's originally from a Belgrade agency. We saw a number of cases where reports were written and quotes were made that may have been or may not have been actually the quotes of what was being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you said had not escaped me. We don't exactly know who is with the Tanjug agency and what is part of the BBC. We don't know if it's Tanjug that ascribes these words to Mr. Prlic or if it's the BBC that is doing the commentary. But just in terms of press, a press agency, when it hears something, it quotes it between -- puts it between inverted commas, and here there's no -- this last sentence, there's no inverted commas or hyphens, so we can assume that it's either the journalist who is making this conclusion or the BBC. What do you think of that? You, in your previous duties, were used to dealing with the press. What is your view on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite specific, when it comes to this text, this is a text produced by the Tanjug news agency from Belgrade. They published it, and then it was carried by the -- by BBC. In my line of work in Bosnia-Herzegovina over the past 15 years, I cannot believe what they're saying in situations of this kind. You saw the text published in "Oslobodjenje" that was tendered in the course of my testimony where some statements were made and some accusations levied against me, and I know that this was not true, but this was a report published by a newspaper that supported one option, and Tanjug supported the option to turn the Republika Srpska into a state. And they used every opportunity to say that Republika Srpska is and should be a state, and regardless of everything else, that was their main goal. And this is why I'm so skeptical about this quote really being attributable to Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I asked you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- few moments ago. We won't come back to it just now, but I mention it so that it is in the context of the question I'm going to put to you, about the absence of substantial armed conflict between the Serbs and the Croats in Herzegovina and most of Central Bosnia through this period, at least the second half of 1993. I just put a marker on that, and I'll come back to it in a moment. Now, is it correct that in accomplishing the Croat goals in the second half of 1993, Mr. Prlic and others in the HVO leadership felt that a military victory over the Muslims was essential, that basically there was no way forward at this time, at least not a good one, for the Croats unless a clear military victory could be achieved over the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this position on the part of Mr. Prlic. I knew that he always said that the conflict should cease as soon as possible, and because the Croats were the smallest community, in the long run they stood no chance in any such conflict, prolonged conflict. This was the way that I saw his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also understood, did you not, that the position of Mr. Prlic and others in the HVO leadership were that Croats should be moved or concentrated from some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina to others, which could be made or would remain, based on those movements, Croat areas?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never considered this as a position of the HVO. The position was that Croats must be helped and that those who leave their homes must be provided with adequate accommodation, alternative housing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P06454. P06454 would be in the second binder. This is a record of a presidential meeting in the offices of President Tudjman on the 5th of November, 1993, and I'd like you to first please turn to page number 30, top of the page, simply if you will to set the scene that we have Mr. Prlic speaking. At the top of page 30, Jadranko Prlic says: "I think that this meeting is extremely important. The highest-ranking officials of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are here, and this is an opportunity for open dialogue on the overall situation that we are in ..." Now, if I can ask you, please, to go to page 36. Toward of the top of that page, and I'll represent to you this is still -- the record will show -- the transcript will show this is still Mr. Prlic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRLIC
utterances.text: "I think that at this moment a military victory is necessary to restore both the situation and the state of mind. I think that it is clear --" excuse me, "I think that is clear and does not need to be explained at all. Whether it is Mostar, whether it is Vakuf or this action that is being planned up there to connect Kiseljak with Busovaca. "We must move closer to rounding off territories. As a government, last spring we defined both the proposals and the conclusions, even with regard to moving certain brigades from some areas, which would include moving the population from those areas and concentrating it in certain directions that we think could become and remain Croatian areas.
