"We would like this solely in the pragmatic sense. I know that the efforts are directed towards every Croat remaining and living where he is now. "But there is pragmatism, there is a concentration of forces, there is everything else. You, as a soldier, know that quite well." Could you please go on to page 38. The bottom of page 38,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRLIC CONTINUES
utterances.text: "As for relations with the other two sides, I am in Velika Kladusa tomorrow, God willing, for talks with these two sides. We must play a game with the Serbs because of these enclaves, because that is the only way to keep them alive at all, and to enable them the military strength to protest themselves against the Muslims." Let me pause there. What Mr. Prlic is talking about here, isn't it correct, sir, is the necessity of Bosnian Croats to move across Serb-held territory; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated that the HVO did not discuss this, the relocation of brigades and so on. This was not a topic that was discussed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me restate my question, sir. Perhaps it was mistranslated or perhaps I misspoke. The reference when Mr. Prlic says: "We must play a game with the Serbs because of these enclaves, because that is the only way to keep them alive at all," he's talking about the necessity of the HVO and Herceg-Bosna authorities and forces to move across Serb-controlled territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it entailed, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "And as for the Muslims, obviously a game will have to be played on two cards, playing different people on one and on the other a card, and probably yourself," referring to President Tudjman, "or some high-ranking official from Croatia will be the one who will unify, who will coordinate that gang." Now, playing two cards with the Muslims, isn't that a little bit like saying one thing one day and saying something different another day?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about, because I was not part of it and I couldn't really explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to challenge you on that. You were a senior member of this government for a period of time. You sat in virtually every meeting of the HVO HZB [sic] during this period. You were a close friend and colleague of Mr. Prlic. I put it to you, sir, you could not -- you cannot tell these Judges that you did not know the policy of the HVO on these matters at that time. Can you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object, and it goes back to my fundamental objection at the beginning. He's asked to comment about a conversation that is taking place where the gentleman was not present. Based on that, unless he's being given an opportunity to read the entire transcript, how is he expected to comment, in light of what he said, he wasn't there and he doesn't know? So that's the fundamental problem that we have here. I understand that the Trial Chamber doesn't wish for the gentleman to take up valuable court time in reading that, but if we want to be fair to the gentleman, then I suggest that either you instruct the Prosecutor to withdraw the question or rephrase it in a manner in which he can answer. But how can he comment about a meeting at which he wasn't present? He's asked to look at a line here and a line there. None of us would be able to do that, even the members of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Mr. Karnavas has unfairly stated my question. It is not uncommon practice, and I'm sure Mr. Karnavas and I dare say every lawyer in this courtroom has done this in this trial, you cite a few examples, you a cite particular example on this occasion. I then worked from the specific to the general, and I challenge Mr. Tomic, given his position, given his close hands-on involvement in these matters throughout this time period, I challenge him that it is not credible for him to say not whether he knew this particular conversation, but the policies of the HVO touching on these topics during this time, and I challenge him that is not a credible situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you knew what the position of the HVO HZ-HB was, didn't you, because you sat in on the meetings, you voted on decisions, you provided the financing? You did all those things, sir, and you cannot sit here and tell these Judges that you did not know what the [indiscernible] of the HVO was during this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please reframe from hitting the podium, because this becomes reinforced for the mic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question -- my apologies for thumping the podium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the objection, I lost the thread. Could you repeat your question to the witness. Let me say that we have a transcript that starts following what happened at [indiscernible]. This is page 1, where Tudjman explains why there's this meeting, and then we don't have pages 2 to 30. And then Mr. Prlic speaking for a few pages, and then it continues, because there are 113 pages, and the document that we have before us is very fragmentary. But speaking from memory, I know that we've already seen this document on various occasions. The Judges are fully informed of the tenor of this document. Before Mr. Scott repeats the question, I just have a minor technical question for you. We have seen several meetings held by Mr. Tudjman that last hours on end. There are dozens of pages. Here we have 100 pages. Is this common practice with you, to have such lengthy meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It all depended on the topic. I attended a couple of meetings that were not that long, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because earlier on we saw a document. I can't remember the number of it, but it was the first meeting with Mr. Susak, starting at 10.00 in the morning and ending at 4.00 in the afternoon. The second meeting with Tudjman, starting at 6.00 in the afternoon, and Tudjman said, "Well, you didn't have anything to eat." So the 6.00 meeting must have lasted into the night, so obviously nobody had a bite to eat. So for participants, it would take the whole day. And this is not the only example. We've seen several documents showing that the meetings would last for hours on end. So it was just a theoretical question, was it useful, or was it customary for you to speak for a long time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as we could see from the transcript, this was an occasion where everybody wanted to say something. That is why it took such a long time. I did not attend many of those meetings. Just one of them lasted a little while longer, but the rest were acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Scott, put the question again, because we lost track of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I must say, Your Honour, it's difficult to conduct -- we're kind of back to some old ways of trying to conduct an examination, and then literally right in the middle of a question, I'm waiting for an answer, and then things go off in another direction, with all respect to the Chamber. I try to lay a foundation, I put the question, and then we move off on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I come back to the question I put to you some time ago that was hanging at the time of the other questions put by the President. Sir, I put to you that you knew full well what the policy of the HVO HZ-HB was during this time period throughout 1993. You sat in on these meetings and you were a close associate and, I dare say, confidant of Mr. Prlic. You attended some of these presidential meetings yourself in Zagreb that we have records of. You knew full well, sir, the policy of the HVO, and you knew that policy was as stated, among other things, in this record that I've just referred you to. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I've already said that the HVO had, as its primary task, the defence and protection of the Croats in the areas that were part of the HZ-HB. That was the concept. That's what I have explained a number of times here in court. I also want to add that at official sessions of the HVO, there was always the same concept. No other concept was ever presented. Of course, peace talks affected the debate, as did the situation on the battlefield. A large number of refugees, things that had to be dealt with on a daily basis, but the policy of the HVO was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've said that repeatedly, but now I come back to the question I put to you a few minutes ago. Are you then suggesting, sir, that -- you say this is what you heard Mr. Prlic say, but I put to you, again, if that's your position, we've now seen a number of instances where Mr. Prlic, I put to you, had said something quite different. I think Mr. Prlic expressed one thing to you and held -- in fact, held on other occasions expressed another view. Is that how the Chamber should understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot offer a judgement on the basis of what I see here. I know that there was a series of situations where pragmatic solutions had to be found in order to resolve this basic political issue that I was talking about. How are we to look at it today, after so many years have passed, I really cannot conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you used the word "pragmatic." Let's go back to page 36, and the Chamber well knows and the lawyers in the courtroom know that these records are transcripts of recordings, of a recording system that was operated in the offices of President Tudjman, and on this day Mr. Prlic is recorded as saying, on page 36: "We must move closer to rounding off territories. As a government, last spring," that would be the spring of 1993, "we defined both the proposals and the conclusions, even with regard to moving certain brigades from some areas, which would include moving the population from those areas and concentrating it in certain directions that we think could become and remain Croatian areas. We would like this solely in the pragmatic sense." Skipping down again: "This is pragmatism." And that's exactly the sort of pragmatic solution that you said just a few moments ago just now was necessary; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this paragraph, I said that I was a member of the Cabinet in spring, not in October when this was going on, but I was in spring. And I know that the government never discussed any programme for the relocation of the brigades or of the population. Now, as to why Mr. Prlic said that, in what circumstances, this is the question that he can answer. I know that at the sessions that I attended, no such positions were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I allowed the witness to answer. I didn't want to object. But as you have said, we don't have all the pages of the minutes here in front of us, and we don't know the context of this debate. Is this a reference to some specific effect, an emergency situation that had to be dealt with, and hence the reaction that is ascribed to Prlic, or is this about the policy in general? We can't say that, on the basis of the minutes that we have. Well, at least we have the date for the minutes, and we could compare it with the events in the field that we talked about here. My learned friend from the Prosecution knows the dates, and he knows the answers that he might expect, but this is out of context here, and the connotation it gets might be completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on page 36 Mr. Prlic said the following. He said: "I believe that a military victory is necessary." We've been working at it for nearly three years, so we know a lot of things. We've heard many witnesses, seen many documents. We know that there was an offensive by the ABiH in Central Bosnia. We know that, unfortunately so, unfortunately for the Croats, they're going to have positions, be it in only in Vares, where there are close to 15.000 Croats, 5 to 15 Croats, they're going to leave Vares. It seems as though the military situation was a very worrying one, and here we have Prlic saying, "I believe that a military victory is necessary." As far as you know, back then in November was the HVO able to prevail in front of the ABiH, or did they need help from the Republic of Croatia? And curiously, oddly enough, I was looking at the document, I was expecting an answer from Tudjman to this question raised by Mr. Prlic, but as a matter of fact, following his intervention, we have Mr. Sancevic speaking. This being said, you were no longer a minister in November. We know that. But from what you know, back then, militarily speaking, was the HVO able to win victory or not? This seems to be called upon by Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you'd asked any Croat at the time, they would all have told you the same thing. A victory was required to regain hope, to stop the flood of refugees, to simply allow people to stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was against this backdrop that the discussion occurred. I really can't say at this point whether the HVO had the military might to achieve that or not, because that was not my area, nor indeed can I judge that sort of issue. I simply don't have sufficient information. I do know one thing, and it's simply enough. Every day, you are being told that people are leaving this town or that town. Under the circumstances, this was something that appeared to us almost as a mission, it being a good idea to improve the atmosphere that prevailed among the Croats and stop the migrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may place a remark on the record. Otherwise, this will head in a different direction. When the witness started answering your question, he said, "I think that all Croats would agree with that," and he also said, "at the time," and he said a victory was required to consolidate. You heard what he said. And what the transcript says, "a victory was required," which might mean the overall victory, but he said something entirely different. And I think this should be clarified with the witness. Otherwise -- well, my learned friend is suggesting that maybe I was premature in this. Well, yes, it seems that the key word was not translated. The witness, at the beginning of his answer, said at the time -- any Croat at the time probably would have said the same thing, that a victory was required. A victory, a victory, in the sense of something being required. [In English] Only one victory is needed, this is what the witness said, only one victory is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you say, exactly, Mr. Tomic? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A victory, a victory, not in the sense of a final victory. A victory somewhere along the frontline, quite simply in order to regain the confidence and for people to stop thinking about leaving. There was panic now, and everyone was preparing to leave their respective areas, especially those in the border areas with the BH Army close by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, in November 1993, as you see it, the morale among the Croats was rather low. They had lost confidence because there was an influx of refugees, there were specific events; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about yourself, were you confident or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a concern that it wouldn't be possible to control the numbers of refugees, in the sense of being able to put them up in the sense of getting sufficient supplies for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question that's just crossed my mind, and then I'll ask Mr. Scott to proceed. In November, Vares was totally evacuated from the Croat population. We've seen documents in which there is mention of the need to put up and send these people everywhere. We've seen several documents to this effect. As far as you know, the Croat -- were the Croat intelligence services aware that there was a major-scale offensive by the ABiH? And in the affirmative, why did they fail to intervene in a transparent and visible way? It may be that you don't know. If you don't know, I'll put the question to the military members that are scheduled to come for other Defence teams, so I could put that question then. But at your level, given the level of disarray, the fact that Croats were leaving in the thousands, why did the Republic of Croatia fail to intervene militarily in a visible and official way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply don't have sufficient information to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll ask the question of military people. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before I begin questioning again and my time with the witness, there's been a number of comments now for some minutes that I've not had a chance to respond to. On the issue of the transcript, Your Honour, and this is not questioning -- this does not go to questioning the witness, you know, we've had this same conversation any number of times. Let me just make a couple of things again clear. The Prosecution's position has been, since Day 1, and it's still the same today, that when the transcripts were admitted, they should have been admitted in toto, partly for these very reasons, so there wouldn't be argument about what's on one page and what's on the previous page. That's been our position all along, it's still our position, and in fact in terms of the recent position by Mr. Karnavas on adding additional material, on much of it I don't think the Prosecution will object, because it's always been our position that the entire transcript should be admitted. Now, having -- which prevents anyone from taking anything out of context. Now, having said that, number 2, as we've said many times, Your Honour, that there's simply no way that we can cover -- read every transcript in full with every witness who comes into this courtroom or that we can put all 120 pages of every transcript in your binders. You have four binders now. How would you like to have ten? How would each of you like to have ten on the Bench, ten binders? These are necessities, this is the way it is, it's the way we've practiced in the last three years, and it is not helpful for anyone to stand up and say, "Well, we've got to read the whole thing, we should have the whole transcript." We just cannot do it, Your Honour, under these circumstances, I put. And the Defence has done exactly the same thing. They've used parts of the transcripts that they wanted to use. The Chamber wants to set days aside which we'll sit and we'll read from page 1 to page 110 of every transcript, but I think the point is made, Your Honour. Now, returning to the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that throughout this time Mr. Prlic -- the topic generally we're talking about is Mr. Prlic's dealings with the Serbs in negotiations during this time period, and you knew, didn't you, that he was engaged in ongoing discussions with the Serbs, especially in the fall of 1993, on a wide range of topics and he was reporting that to the HVO HZ-HB, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about some of his contacts with the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, you knew that he was at one point negotiating agreements with something called the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, associated with someone named Fikret Abdic, and also with the Serb Republic or RS, involving Mr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't up to date on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to Exhibit P10707 in binder number 3, P10707. Sir, while you have that and -- this is an article reported by the BBC again on the 9th of November, 1993. Given some of the things that were mentioned earlier, I note that the source of this article originally apparently was the Croatian TV Satellite Service in Croatia given at 1830 Greenwich Mean Time on the 7th of November, 1993. Now, Mr. Prlic, in this discussion -- or in this article, there is discussions about his meetings involved with these individuals and the entities that they represented, including Mr. Lukic, the prime minister of the RS, and there's also reference to his giving his support to a joint statement issued by Fikret Abdic and the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, and the declaration signed in Belgrade by Abdic and Karadzic. Now, were you familiar with all those negotiations and signed documents in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you recall Mr. Prlic reporting back during the meetings around this time about these negotiations, about his dealings with the Serbs and about the dealings with Mr. Abdic's authorities, so-called?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the government at the time. Therefore, I can't remember whether this was, in fact, the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wasn't it true, sir, that throughout this time period again, Mr. Prlic was in regular and frequent communication with the Bosnian Serb leadership, including travel to the various locations to meet with them, by use of the telephone, by use of the fax? Mr. Prlic was having extensive dealings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent this was an ongoing contact. I know about the visit to Banja Luka, I know about what the media said, but I have no idea about whether the nature of this was ongoing or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you know that he was involved, again, with negotiating prisoner exchanges with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mention a while ago, when we talked about that report, that there was a lot of pressure being exerted by families, by people from Kupres who were in captivity. There was a lot of pressure for them to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, to go to Exhibit P06581, P06581, in binder number 2. Binder number 2, 06581. This is a record of another presidential meeting in Zagreb on the 10th of November, 1993. And, Usher, if you can assist us by taking the witness to page 3. At the top of that page, President Tudjman starts by saying: "Did you have a meeting by Karadzic?" Mate Boban: "No. Tomorrow is the government meeting." Then going on to Jadranko Prlic: "It was like this. I went up there. There was some complications in crossing," et cetera, et cetera. "When I arrived in Banja Luka in the evening, there was change and some talks, and we sent that fax" - and given some issues raised about communications, I underline the word "fax" - "Which said that it was today on Thursday." Going on down: "The told me they received it on Sunday, that Komarcia [phoen], Komarica," excuse me, my apologies for pronunciation, "wrote that part by hand, that things to be further clarified over the phone. On Sunday evening, I was down there in Kladusa, down there according to their statements," et cetera. Now, if you go to page 7, please, page 7, again Jadranko Prlic: "As regards these Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that exchange was going on with them. We agreed on that, you know that, and they have delivered their part." And then he goes on talking about the Croats to Banja Luka: "This is work obligation and they cannot be prevented in that. They pick apples, and that's better than their going to the army. There, those are some of the essential things." Now, sir, I'm wondering, based on some of the answers you've given us in the last few minutes, is it your position or is it your understanding, based on seeing this, that Mr. Prlic reported more information about his dealings to President Tudjman in Zagreb than he reported to the HVO government in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't conclude that based on this. For as long as I was a government member, we had information on what Mr. Prlic knew, and for a while after that I was no longer a member of the government and I really can't comment in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to end this section, if you will, by going back to the question I put to you some minutes ago now, and based on having seen and been through a number of additional documents. Isn't it correct, sir, that by February 1994, there had been no substantial armed clashes between the Bosnian Serbs and the Croats for at least the preceding seven months?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say exactly, in relation to that period, about these military operations, as I pointed out before. I know, for example, when there were clashes at Usora, but what the extent of those clashes was or the exact timing, I really can't say. It wasn't my duty to keep track of those clashes. I do know, however, that at Usora there was information relating to an attempt to put a stop to the Serbs' breakthrough, but I really can't put up a timeline for you that you could rely on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you also know around February, the first part of 1994, that Mr. Prlic was negotiating with the Serbs to -- Bosnian Serbs to connect the power transmission lines of both the Croats and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say, in relation to this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at P10705.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm still on this meeting. We'll, of course, have the opportunity to return with other witnesses to this document, but it's an important document, because this meeting is held on the 10th of November, 1993, and plainly we discover two things; that Mr. Tudjman knew absolutely nothing about the Stupni Do matter, asking who this rage [as interpreted] is and then the destruction of the old bridge. It's the same position by Tudjman, who inquires and who asks questions. Now, in your view, was Mr. Tudjman well informed of what was happening in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think he did have sufficient information available to him. I don't know about the quality of his information, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're assuming that he had the information, but you can't say anything further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say, because that wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, looking, please, at P10705, an article again from the BBC Monitoring Service, 15 February 1994, this reports Mr. Prlic's involvement in negotiating an agreement to connect the power transmission lines. And because of the time factor, what I particularly want to direct your attention to is the third paragraph, where it is stated in this article -- actually, the information is attributed to the Bosnian Serb leader, Lukic: "There have been no clashes between Bosnian Serbs and Croats already for all of seven months, which is an example of how clashes can be avoided in war, Lukic stressed." And I put to you one final time, Mr. Tomic: Don't you know and isn't it a fact that this statement by Mr. Lukic is correct, that as of February 1994, there had not been any substantial clashes between the Bosnian Serbs and the Croats for the previous seven months?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question a number of times already. I don't have the timeline, and I can't confirm that. I know that there were clashes at Usora, but I cannot define a timeline for you exactly as to how and when this went on. I do know that this was a place where for a long time there were clashes between us and the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, changing topics, unless there's any follow-up questions from the Judges on that last document or two, changing topics, sir, to -- going back to some things we touched on earlier last time, but I want to tie back in to some other questions I want to put to you, please. Sir, you may recall that we looked at a number of documents the last time, including one of the records of the Livno meeting from the 9th of February, 1992. And I suggest we don't need to look at it, but for the record, in particular, P00117, which you saw last time and which I think the Judges have seen a number of times. Sir, the language of the referendum that the people in attendance of that meeting voted for, the formulation they wanted was -- it said the following: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a joint state of the constituted and sovereign Croatian, Muslim and Serbian peoples in their own ethnic areas (cantons)?" That was the formulation that the HDZ central board meeting in Livno on the 9th of February, 1992, that's what they wanted; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that continued to be, sir, was it not, the position of the HVO and Herceg-Bosna authorities throughout this time period, 1992, 1993, into 1994, was an organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of separate ethnic areas, so the Croats would have their area, the Serbs would have their area, and the Muslims would have their area? Wasn't that the desired model?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't define these as pure ethnic areas with Serbs, Muslims, or Croats alone in them. We were discussing majority areas populated predominantly by one, the other, or the third ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Three ethnic areas, not necessarily pure, but three ethnic areas, that was the desired structure; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to go to Exhibit P00498. P00498, which will be in the first binder. Sir, this is another record of a presidential meeting in Zagreb on the 17th of September, 1992. I'd like to direct your attention, please, to page 26. On page 26, Mr. Prlic states to those assembled: "I want to say that we are holding firm on the lines of defence of the Croatian territories in Herceg-Bosna. I have exact information here about the Bosnian Posavina which has formally not yet been associated into Herceg-Bosna. We're going abroad tomorrow, and we shall solve these questions too. At this moment, due to a shortage of technical means, we are not ready for offensive operations, especially in regard to Kupres," et cetera. "Otherwise, we are holding firm on the line which is over 500 kilometres long." Sir, in your experience, and this was true at the HVO HZ-HB meetings, was it not, Mr. Prlic was quite well informed on the military situation, and in fact in this situation he could provide quite specific information to President Tudjman, couldn't he? "Due to a shortage of technical means, we are not ready for offensive operations. Otherwise, we are holding firm on the line which is over 500 kilometres long." Now, you told us the last time that -- let me just put something further and I'll come back to you. You told us the last time you were here, sir, when I asked you about Mr. Prlic's management style, you said he was a man who dotted his "i"s and crossed his "t"s. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that these are my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I asked you that question, sir, and I believe the record will show that you said, yes, Mr. Prlic was a talented administrator, paid attention to detail. And I believe I put to you, and if we had the time I would put to you the transcript page, I put it to you he was the kind of person who crossed his "t"s and dotted his "i"s, and I believe, sir, that you agreed. But in any event, you would agree, would you not, that Mr. Prlic in fact was well informed about the military situation in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall this phrase, whether I used this phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is an attempt to confuse the witness. This phrase, to dot the "i"s and cross the "t"s, this is not something that was said by the witness, but this was -- this was quite properly translated in this way, however. But now this is an effort to confuse the witness, because the phrase that is used in Croatian is not something that is inherent in our language. The witness's words were translated in an appropriate manner into English, but now when they are back-translated, they are confusing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say is that the quote, as it was given back to me by the Prosecutor, this was not something that I said. This was not the phrase that I used, because I don't say to dot the "i"s in my language. And now whether this is a conclusion of my discussion of my position, it's a completely different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could, the question was posed by Mr. Scott in that fashion. I know for a fact that he -- that he -- but obviously it might have been -- something was lost in translation. But I can verify that Mr. Scott did, in fact -- asked the question whether he was the sort of person that crossed his "t"s and dotted his "i"s. Now, whether -- and as I recall the answer, Mr. Tomic did say that he did cross his "t"s, something to that effect, and I can find the passage. I read it yesterday, in fact. But, again, something must have been lost in translation. But the problem is, I think, is that the witness objects to a question being formulated by the Prosecutor, then being turned out -- then the Prosecutor claiming that this is the witness's words. I think that's where the confusion may lie. I'm not ascribing any, you know, ill intention on either side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, thank you, thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I know, indeed, Mr. Scott and the Defence, Mr. Kovacic, this is a dispute of words with no relevance at all. You can very well ask Mr. Scott, well, do you want to ask without using this image?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, before I do that, Your Honour, before I do that, there has been so much about -- discussion about -- and I do appreciate and thank Mr. Karnavas for his candour in indicating that I did, in fact, put the question. In the record at 34105-106, the question was put -- and, Mr. Tomic, just so you can put your own mind at ease, you may want to listen to this as well. Question: "All right. Well, my question to you is focusing more on Mr. Prlic than the premises of the -- the premises or the operation of the office. Would you say, in your experience, that Mr. Prlic is a very -- in fact a very competent, in fact very talented administrator?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Would it be fair so say that Mr. Prlic is the type of person who we might say -- and, forgive me, I don't know if it will -- I don't know if you have it in your language, but we might say the type of person who dots his 'i's and dots his 't's?" Answer: "Yes, that's what he always tries to do, to dot his 'i's and crosses his 't's." Witness's own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it is not the witness's own words; it is the translation, and we have many times made the experience that a good translator will translate one figure of speech to a corresponding but not literally identical figure of speech in another language, and another interpreter will then maybe translate back by using the figure of speech which he translates, and then it's uncomprehensible. So I really think go on and let's forget about the "i"s and the "t"s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Judge Trechsel, I'm sorry, but, you know, this is the trial record, what it says, whatever we have. Is there anyone who doubts the content or the concept of what was put to the witness and what the answer was? He was a talented administrator who paid attention to detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we agree on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to confirm what Judge Trechsel has just said. This is the first time, two minutes ago, that this phrase, in the English language, was translated literally into Croatian, to dot the "i"s and cross the "t"s, and the witness has not yet heard it yet in courtroom. This was the first time that he heard it. I think that we really have to cut this whole debate short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We spent ten minutes. Witness, the question was very simple. Was Mr. Prlic informed of the military situation? That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that a certain volume of information was available through the joint meetings that we had. But as for the operations themselves, the planning, as far as I know, he did not have any information about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate, Your Honours, the assistance of so many, and I will move on without belabouring the point further. I hope the point is clear, regardless of the particular metaphor that one might use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me direct your attention on to page 28 of that same document. Excuse me a moment. Sir, continuing on, on page 28 Mr. Prlic gives essentially a rundown of the various positions of the three parties, actually: "The Serbs want an association of states in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That practically means no state regarding Bosnia and Herzegovina. What would exist at the centre would be financed, and any state based on this is no state. That is the Serbs' option. The Muslims' option is what the previous speakers suggested, said, but essentially and personally, it is a civic and unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is what we all personally think." Then he goes down below and he talks about the Croat position: "The Croats, at least the soldiers in the Croatian Defence Council and the people who are involved, the organs of authority, have a clear political aim. It has been clear to me ever since I became involved in this and since I have been in this post, that is, the constituting of Bosnia and Herzegovina through three national units. Now, sir, that's fully consistent with the language of the Livno formulation, if you will, that I put to you a few moments ago, correct, three national units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he does -- Mr. Prlic does say "with the principles of the European Community." That's in the text, keeping in mind that it is the European Community that is driving the negotiating formulas. And this is a critical aspect of what he's saying. So if we're going to pose that question, perhaps it should be added, "Did Dr. Prlic promote the initiatives of the internationals, especially the International Community, with respect to how Bosnia and Herzegovina should internally be formulated?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is argument and commentary. This is exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Scott -- this is a place where it is really easy to put in the full quotation, and that's what Mr. Karnavas -- so I would say let's not quarrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy to read it entirely, Your Honour. Everyone in the courtroom has it. I'm sorry, no, there is no misleading anyone in the courtroom about it. But, you know -- well: "Since I became involved in this and since I have been in this post, this aim is the forming and ordering of Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with the principles of the European Community, that is, the constituting of Bosnia-Herzegovina through three national units." Now, having read the entire thing, it's still my position what Mr. Karnavas says is argument and commentary in front of the witness, and that is my position. He says that, but that's his position. And I'm not suggesting that the Prosecution agrees with that, or the witness, for that matter. We don't know. So there's no reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, my question to you was specifically: That was what follows dead on, the formulation as expressed by the HDZ central board gathered in Livno on the 9th of February, 1992, the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in three separate ethnic units or, as said here, three national units; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add to this, that I have already --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not fully, not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. How many times, again, in the last two and a half years and during the Prosecution case did Mr. Karnavas say, "Answer the question, yes or no," and I think I'm entitled to the same process as was afforded to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My first -- I'll give you -- I'll let you clarify, sir, I'll let you add, but my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try and answer as the question was put to you, even if you don't like it, but that's it, because in the case of the redirect the Prosecutor is entitled to put a leading question that answers "yes" or "no," "I don't agree," or "I don't know," and then according to your answer, depending on your answer, the Prosecutor may supplement if need be. Mr. Scott, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is the third time -- at least the third time I've asked you this question. The formulation put forward here by Mr. Prlic on the 17th of September, 1992, some nine months after the meeting in Livno in February, that -- those formulations are, for all practical purposes, the same, aren't they? Three national units, each people in their own separate ethnic areas (cantons), three national units; correct? It's the same basic structure, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because here it is through and not in separate units inhabited by only one people. And in the minutes, it goes on to say that the only criterion will not be the ethnic composition of the population. We should also take into account geographic elements, transportation. So we're not talking about -- the goal is not ethnically-pure units, so this is the context where I differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we already had this discussion. You corrected me, yourself, or you suggested earlier that the Livno question was similar, that it didn't necessarily mean pure ethnic areas but three primarily, you said a few minutes ago -- again, if we have to take the time to go back in the transcript, what the Livno question was calling for was majority ethnic areas. Now, that's exactly the qualification you gave 20 or 30 minutes ago, and that's the same qualification you can make now, if you want. Nobody in the courtroom said "ethnically pure," but the structure was three national units, correct? Or do you not believe what Mr. Prlic says on the 17th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what was said here was, but the entirety of what was said was the policy pursued by the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on to page 29 -- Your Honour, I think we may be coming up on a break, but perhaps I can finish with this document, if the Court will allow. Sir, if you can on to page 29, just a few more items, or one or two more items from this, this is Mr. Prlic continuing, and toward the bottom part, not exactly the bottom, but toward the bottom of that page, you'll find this passage at the end of one of the paragraphs: "There is still no political agreement regarding the relations between the Croats and the Muslims. These relations," and again we're talking September 1992. "These relations are becoming ever more tense and certain conflicts are looming. Personally, I think it would be impossible to avoid conflicts entirely." And he goes on about trying to send some letters, et cetera. Now, isn't that a position not only held by Mr. Prlic at that time, but didn't you and others in the HVO leadership hold similar views? You knew, based upon the positions being taken around this time, that essentially a conflict between the Croats and the Muslims was virtually inevitable, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not about the military conflict, the way I see it. At that time in our day-to-day work, we saw the reactions and we encountered conflicts when it came to the implementation of the regulations on the ground. In all the segments, finance, justice, et cetera, there were tensions, and that caused problems. And this is the way I see it, in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you'd like to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Registrar, how much does the Prosecutor have left? Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to next, please, look at Exhibit P10701 in the third binder. P10701. And while you're looking at that, sir, this is again a BBC Monitoring Service publication dated the 26th of April, 1993. My question to you is this: In about the middle of that -- there's only about two paragraphs. In the second paragraph, it says: "The president of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Jadranko Prlic, spoke about the latest clashes between the HVO and Muslim forces at today's press conference (one of the regular HVO press conferences held in Mostar every day)." Were you familiar with the general practice of the HVO authorities to, in fact -- can you confirm that there was something like a daily press conference?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not held on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately how often?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you exactly, but I know that the HVO HZ-HB did not hold those conferences all that often. After our sessions, there were press releases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who were the principal spokespersons for the HVO HZ-HB at these press conference -- press conferences?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that you couldn't even say "principal spokespersons," because there were not many of those press conferences. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put to you that they were, in fact, much more regular than you apparently indicate. Apart from Mr. Prlic, who else would speak at these conferences?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at P10706. This is a BBC article dated the 6th of May, 1993, based on a story coming out of the Croatian TV Satellite Service in Zagreb about the launch of Croatian Radio Herceg-Bosna, says it was marked in Mostar today, the 4th of May: "In the presence of the president of Herceg-Bosna, HVO, Jadranko Prlic and several other HVO officials, radio director Zlatko Prienda stressed that all transmitters, which would enable Croatian Radio of Herceg-Bosna to be heard throughout Bosnia would be erected in the next few weeks." Again, sir, wasn't it the case that at press releases, press conferences, statements to the media such as this, Mr. Prlic was very often the person involved in making such statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, do you recall that it was indeed around this time, early May 1993, when further steps were taken to establish and operate something called the Croatian Radio of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian Radio of Herceg-Bosna was established by a decision of the HVO HZ-HB in order to broadcast information throughout the HZ-HB, in light of the fact that up until that time there were mostly local radio stations active there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you recall, do you not, that around -- we talked about this, the meeting -- the HVO HZ-HB meeting on the 3rd of April, 1993, and you agree, do you not, that around the 3rd of April, 1993, Herceg-Bosna, the HVO authorities, issued what became was -- or became known as an ultimatum to armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina to either subordinate themselves to the HVO or to leave those areas, so-called Croat areas, by the 15th of April, 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was within the framework of the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you knew, did you not, that there were a number of documents and conditions in connection with President Izetbegovic's signature of that document which had not yet been resolved; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the correspondence between Mr. Prlic and Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, though, and if we can look -- if I can direct your attention to P10675, P10675 in the third binder, please. And while you're looking at that, sir, I'll just tell you and I'll say for the purposes of the record, this is a collection of four articles, one dated the 4th of April, 1993, from Reuters News, a second one from Financial Times, dated 20 April 1993, one from the Christian Science Monitor dated 7 April 1993, and one from Agence France-Presse on the 16th of April, 1993, all reporting on what's described in, I believe, each of the articles as the HVO ultimatum with the deadline 15th of April, 1993. Let me direct your particular attention, please, because of the time limitations that we have. If you can go to the Christian Science Monitor article, which is, I believe, sir, the third article in your binder -- in that bundle, please, excuse me. Toward the end of that -- well, about two-thirds through the overall article, at the bottom of the English version on the first page, for those reading in English, it says: "Mr. Prlic concedes, nonetheless, that the HVO ultimatum could lead to bloodshed. 'We expect everything. We don't want this struggle, we don't have any reason for this struggle,' he says." Would you agree with that statement, in terms of further confirming that there was, indeed, this ultimatum, and would you confirm -- would you confirm and agree with Mr. Prlic, that it was known, given the circumstances, that quote, anything -- something to the effect of, excuse me, anything could happen?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think that this was an ultimatum. That's not how I see it. I consider this to be a step in the direction of the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. And this was not Prlic, the president of the HVO, as indicated in this text, but as the prime minister, as he was designated at the time. The situation was difficult already at that time, and it was expected that the signatories of the agreement would make an effort to implement this, and the statement made by the Defence minister that followed later, Mr. Rajic, must also be seen in this context. So I don't think that this was an ultimatum with an ultimate goal of causing a conflict. This was more -- I just wanted to say that this was mostly an expression of the desire to implement this agreement as soon as possible and to move over to another stage in the activities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you may not want to use the term "ultimatum," sir, but you would agree, would you not, that it was the statement of a position with a deadline, the deadline being the 15th of April, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we go back to the first article before we need to move on, the Reuters article, the fifth paragraph on that page in that article says: "The HVO set an April 15 deadline for Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic to sign a joint communique ratifying the withdrawals, creating a common high command and certifying there were no Muslim-Croat territorial disputes." And skipping a paragraph, it says: "If Izetbegovic fails to sign this agreement by April 15th, the HVO will unilaterally enforce its jurisdiction in Cantons 3, 8 and 10, the statement from the HVO headquarters in the southwest Croat stronghold of Mostar warned." Now, those are both true and accurate statements, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the latter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on, sir, to the so-called Medjugorje Agreement which you spent some time discussing with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, we just saw that there were three press releases, and my eye was caught by the AFP release in Zagreb. Usually, the AFP is a very precise news agency. I find here that the HVO had a spokesperson, Mr. Veso Vegar, and allegedly this person said, and this is being quoted by the AFP agency, that this is resolutely an ultimatum. "We can't wait indefinitely until the peace plan is implemented." So the HVO spokesperson says here that this is an ultimatum, and you said it wasn't. Well, did you know this Mr. Veso Vegar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. However, Mr. Veso Vegar was not a spokesperson for the HVO HZ-HB. He was a spokesperson of the military component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was a spokesperson for the military component. I see. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one question further on that. When you say this spokesman for the military component, Mr. Vegar was the spokesperson for the HVO Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he wasn't with the HVO HZ-HB. We had a service that was run by another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you'll answer my question, sir. You were there in Mostar throughout this time period. You were one of the central figures in the Herceg-Bosna government. You knew Mr. Vegar, and you knew, sir, did you not, that he was the spokesperson for the HVO Main Staff? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, unless there's additional questions, Your Honours, I'll move on to the next topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you started -- I made reference just a few moments ago to the Medjugorje Agreement, and let's just try to clarify a few things. There's a reference to "Medjugorje Agreement," but isn't it correct, sir, that at least on the political or governmental side, at best, there were some conceptual discussions at the meeting on the 18th of May, 1993, which never, and I emphasise the word "never," resulted in a signed written agreement?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any details regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you -- excuse me, sir. You testified about this at length in response to questions from Mr. Karnavas. Now, you knew then but you don't know now, or how do you explain the fact that you could talk about it when you were here ten days ago, but now you don't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if perhaps the question was rephrased. I mean, how is one to interpret what are the conceptual discussions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is exactly -- I mean, if you could be more concrete, perhaps the gentleman might be able to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll try, thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was simply, I think, rather simple, and was ultimately this, sir: Isn't it correct, at least on the political or governmental side, there was never a signed written agreement? I put it to you, sir, that there was one meeting on the 18th of May. Certain discussions were had, and concept. There was never any signed written agreement; yes or no? There either was or there wasn't. There's nothing in between.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is something that is called the Medjugorje Agreement, then probably there was an agreement like that. I inferred this based on the correspondence between Mr. Prlic and Mr. Izetbegovic. Mr. Izetbegovic invokes the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Has anyone ever shown you a document that says this is the Medjugorje Agreement with the signatures of the parties? Not "probably, there probably was one." Did you ever see one?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen a document like that. And the same applies to a million other documents or agreements that were there and that we were being informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, you would agree, would you not, just on these things generally, that what was being discussed, the establishment of governments and structures, there were many loose ends, if you will, and again I guess I'm not sure how that will translate, unresolved items remaining after the meeting on the 18th of May, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe you testified that one of the things you were critical about was that you were critical of Mr. Izetbegovic and the Muslims for wanting to start work at the provincial level first, instead of concerning the central government. But I put it to you, sir, wasn't that exactly the same position as Mate Boban, that Mr. Boban wanted to start with the provincial governments, just as Mr. Izetbegovic did? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What context?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of any discussions to go forward with anything -- the concepts discussed on the 18th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing that wasn't questioned was the establishment of authorities in the cantons. What was questioned was the resolution of the previous issue, which was the establishment of state authorities, who will bankroll the army, who will bankroll the police, and how the breakdown in terms of authority between the cantons and the central government. And this is the one issue that was not resolved. As for establishing the cantons themselves, all this meant was destruction of the HZ-HB, but not the establishment of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the Vance-Owen Plan, and that is why this activity had to be coordinated and a government had to be set up which the cantons would then communicate with in terms of defining their respective authorities down to the minutest detail. It wasn't just about setting up cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly, sir, and none of those things are resolved at one meeting on the 18th of May, 1993, were they, and they never were resolved because there never was an agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have this meeting with several people in it. You can't expect them to deal with a question such as establishing a state. That is why you need a government. They have to communicate with other levels, other authorities, and that brings the whole thing to a conclusion. You can't just expect an agreement to define all the details that need defining. The Washington Agreement or the Dayton Accords were not successful in this, either, on their own. It wasn't until later on when the government started operating that amendments were made to both the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, for exactly the reasons you just stated, for exactly those reasons, there were so many things left unresolved, so many issues still to resolve, based on one meeting, one day's meeting. Wasn't it a bit premature for Jadranko Prlic to start sending letters describing himself as the president of this so-called new government?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't premature. Mr. Izetbegovic himself, when he replied, behaved this way. His name was nominated, he was put forward. Some personnel decisions at a later stage in Washington had also been pre-agreed, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we don't have time to go through all the documents. I put to you again, as you agreed just a few minutes ago, there was a discussion and concept on one day, on the 18th of May, 1993, which never resulted in any actual agreement, including any position held by Mr. Prlic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to -- I object. This has been asked and it's been answered. The gentleman did indicate that Izetbegovic had responded to correspondence to Dr. Jadranko Prlic based exactly on this particular agreement and nominations that he was asking for, the sort of positions or ministries that Izetbegovic wished to have, and there was correspondence to that. So I think we can move on. This horse has been beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with Mr. Karnavas, Your Honour. He may think it's beaten to death, but I don't have to accept his position on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do put your question, because there were exchanges of letters between Mr. Prlic and Mr. Izetbegovic on this subject. Well, the Prosecution has a specific point of view. Put it forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I agree with that, Mr. President. I'd agree that there was correspondence. We saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can look, please, sir, at 1D 01597. It will be in the fourth binder, excuse me, so-called Defence binder. 1D 01597. Sir, if you have that document, 1D 01597, this is one of the letters that I think Mr. Karnavas showed you dated the 23rd of May, 1993. Now, just on some of the items we've just been talking about, if you look at the very beginning of Mr. Prlic's letter, Mr. Prlic starts out, in fact, by saying: "Although I have only been verbally informed of the decisions made at the meeting in Medjugorje ..." Sir, doesn't what Mr. Prlic say there only a few days later, on the 23rd of May, after the 18th of May, doesn't that in fact suggest to you that there was no agreement or there was no written agreement, because even Mr. Prlic himself says, "I've only been verbally informed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. How can he answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, but look at the question, Your Honour. I mean, how does he come up with this, that there was no agreement based on that he was verbally informed? One can be verbally informed of an agreement or informed in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. "Although I have only been verbally informed," does that not suggest, sir, that Mr. Prlic had not, by that time, seen a written -- a signed, written agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, he didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, then in the -- down below in about the third paragraph, he says: "I have prepared new facilities for the government offices, since I am of the opinion that it cannot operate in existing conditions in occupied Sarajevo." So, Mr. Prlic presumes to move this new government out of Sarajevo. The next -- skipping one paragraph: "If I don't receive responses from the representatives of the nations in the established time frame (Mr. Mate Boban has expressed interest in the ministries of international trade)," et cetera, "I will be forced to inform you to that effect." Sir, isn't this one more instance that the Chamber has heard, these Judges have heard a number of -- and seen a number of instances of the HVO jumping the gun, getting way ahead of itself on where things actually stood at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before he answers that question, he should be given the opportunity to look at 1D 01600, which is Izetbegovic responding to Dr. Jadranko Prlic. You have to read both of them together. And having given the witness the opportunity to read both of them together, then he can pose that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Perhaps I can conduct my examination and Mr. Karnavas can conduct his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're entitled to. The Trial Chamber is aware of all the documents, because it has reviewed them all. But you could have asked the question differently. You could have asked the witness whether he had already seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't my question, Your Honours. That's why I didn't put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was, sir: Isn't this another instance of the HVO, we would say, and again whatever the Croatian translation might be, jumping the gun, acting prematurely on things where there was no -- in fact no agreement yet reached, in fact, and there never was?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that this was merely an active approach to the implementation of that agreement. It also expressed a desire to see the Vance-Owen Plan implemented, as well as to stop the clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go, sir, to Exhibit P02613, P02613, in the second -- no, sorry, first binder. P02613. This is a record of another meeting in the offices of President Tudjman on the 2nd of June, 1993, and on this particular occasion, according to this record, President Tudjman, Defence Minister Susak and perhaps others were meeting with perhaps, among others, Lord David Owen. And I would like to direct your attention, please, in particular to -- excuse me a moment, my apologies -- starting at page 10. Starting at page 10, Mr. Owen says: "We analysed the confederal solution which actually divides Bosnia into three parts. However, in this way we haven't managed to find a way to establish a viable Muslim state. You would in fact create some kind of Palestine. They would never accept it and they would continue to fight." Then going over to the top of the next page, Tudjman says: "Who would never accept it, Europe or Lord Owen?" "The Muslims, the Muslims would never accept it." And then toward -- at the end of that page, jumping down, he says: "But, whenever I analyse the tripartite division of BH, I think it does not give enough to the Muslims. I think your people would want to take more than they should or what the rest of the world would allow them," next page, "that's one thing. It's enough to look at how Boban interprets the provinces of Travnik and Mostar. He speaks about them as if they were his, and that's how he started to behave. They were not his. These are the provinces in which he will probably have certainly a majority in the province of Mostar and probably a majority in the province of Travnik." And then going on to page 13, in the middle of the page, Owen says: "I wouldn't want to give up on the idea to preserve BH, but I'm certainly prepared to consider a possibility, if that is not possible, to establish a viable Muslim state." Tudjman: "As far as we are concerned, we too can influence the Croats, but not slowly. We can influence the Croats to accept this confederal. So to apply the Vance-Owen Plan with regard to the Croats along those lines, such as Provinces 3, 8 and 10, this is roughly what in 1939 became part of the banovina of Croatia." Now, sir, when we go back, again I wanted to read a broader part so that I wouldn't be accused of reading too little, but didn't -- isn't Owen at the top of page 12 telling Tudjman, once again, "You've jumped --" you know, "Boban, you've jumped the gun. You've acted like this is something that's already happened when in fact it hasn't happened"? Isn't that, sir, the case with the way you've described the so-called Medjugorje Agreement? Sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not about the provinces. This is about the establishment of state authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the Vance-Owen Plan. It's not merely about the cantons. It's about the overall authority being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've intervened with you very, very little today, but I'm putting the language to you specifically at the top of page 12. Now, please, please assist me to this extent. Look exactly at the language, what Owen says: "It is enough to look at how Boban interprets the provinces of Travnik and Mostar. He speaks about them as if they were his, and that's how he started to behave." That's my question. And that's, in fact, what happened, isn't it? I mean, isn't that what happened in January 1993, in April 1993, in May 1993? Sir, the HVO was always jumping the gun and doing what they want to do, but there's no agreement to that effect; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is the case. This is based on the Vance-Owen Plan, and the plan was confirmed. Therefore, this is nothing more than an active role in terms of the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. I declare that at the time the Muslim side was not interested in its full implementation, simply because they didn't know what the fate would be of the Bosnia-Herzegovina in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I put it to you, sir, that when you say that the Muslim side was not interested in its full implementation, what you should say, sir, and I put to you is the correct position, is that the Muslims did not agree with the implementation as conceived by the HVO. Isn't that the correct statement?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P10698, P10698 in the binder number 3. Sir, this is an article -- a Reuters article dated the 28th of October, 1992. And we've gone back a bit in time, but for a reason. This is again starting with a discussion about Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance. About halfway down the first page, you'll see a paragraph, I believe, that says: "But Jadranko Prlic, president of the republic declared by Croats in the area of Bosnia they control, told Reuters that the only way to achieve a stable solution was to have three national units, whose parts need not be physically connected." Now, sir, again, doesn't this take us back to and can we agree again that the position of the HVO and the Herceg-Bosna authorities, as seen in Livno, as seen in other documents that we've looked at when you were here before and again today, that the basic position was and remained the establishment of separate ethnic areas? Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that there is this question that had been going on since Livno. It was not about ethnically-pure areas. There was some options, such as the cantons, on the one hand, or a unit, on the other, that physically --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... specific. I'm talking about this article and the statement attributed to Jadranko Prlic, not what your own thoughts were at the time. Did Jadranko Prlic say then and continue to say throughout this period that the solution was three national units? Nobody said that they were 100 per cent pure ethnic, anything about that. You continually say that. You said it about five times today. The idea was three ethnic units, and that's what Mr. Prlic told Reuters in October 1992, and that continued to be the HVO position, didn't it? Yes?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit P10532, P10532 in the third binder. This is a BBC article dated the 9th of August, 1993, apparently based on an interview with someone named Miomir Zuzul. You knew Mr. Zuzul, didn't you, and he was -- in his position at the time in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you look at the third paragraph of Mr. -- well, excuse me, the article and the statements attributed to Mr. Zuzul, can you recall, sir, that it was around this time, by August 1993 and the fall of 1993, that there began to be discussion of another model, since the Muslims had not agreed to three separate areas, of something that became known or would ultimately become known as a Croat-Muslim federation?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't up to date on those activities at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the third paragraph, it says: "Asked why the Muslim idea of unification of Muslim and Croat republics into a Bosnian and Herzegovinian union is not acceptable, Zuzul said, 'it could hardly work,' and that it would be to the benefit of the third side, that is, of Serbia." Do you remember -- do you recall that view being expressed, not only by Mr. Zuzul but in general by the Croat side, in August and following, 1993, that the idea of a joint Croat-Muslim unit, if you will, was not feasible, it could hardly work?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you have to look at the entire paragraph, Your Honours, and the witness should also look at the very last line, because it would drive the Serbs, you know, into the hands of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that's why, because then that would mean, you know, the carve-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what it's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're commenting now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're right. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'm going to -- there have been relatively few interventions, but I'm going to object to that. I mean, that's Mr. Karnavas testifying. He can state an objection, but it's not for him to argue what he thinks the document says, or means, or what it should mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you remains. I'll just simply read it back to you. Do you recall that view being expressed not only by Mr. Zuzul but generally on the Croat side in August and following, 1993, that the idea of a joint Croat-Muslim unit, if you will, was not feasible or, Mr. Zuzul's words, "it could hardly work"?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't up to date or up to speed on that, on the community being created at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise for this intervention, but I believe there is a misunderstanding that has just occurred. My learned friend Mr. Scott asked a question about a joint Croat-Muslim unit, whereas Mr. Zuzul is talking about the unity of the two republics, the Muslim and the Croat. Therefore, there is no talk here of a single Croat-Muslim unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Counsel.
