In the paragraph it says -- in the third paragraph, it says: "Asked why the Muslim idea of unification," making one, "of Muslim and Croat republics into a Bosnia-Herzegovina union," being one, "is not acceptable." I do believe that was the question put to Mr. Zuzul and to which Mr. Zuzul says "It could hardly work."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, coming back to your previous answer, and -- sir, how can you say -- how can you, as a member of this government, the finance minister or the head of the finance department, and once again a very close colleague and confidant of Mr. Prlic, someone who the HVO HZ-HB minutes would indicate was heavily involved in these matters, how can you say you wouldn't know what the position of the HVO was at the time on these matters which had to be, had to be, sir, of great importance to you and the leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what the position of the HVO was. You asked me about the position of Mr. Zuzul and other Croatian or Croat officials. I thought you were referring to other officials from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, sir, if that was the cause of confusion. I'm talking about the HVO Herceg-Bosna leadership, those who were in the government that you sat on in Mostar throughout 1993. Wasn't that the position of the HVO government?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our position was Bosnia and Herzegovina, through three units or through cantons with ethnic majority populations, and from the beginning until the end this was the position in the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Didn't you --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, variants --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's okay, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during this time, and we're now moving into the fall of 1993, isn't it correct, sir, and I just want to put this general proposition to you and I'll try to do it as clearly as I can - please listen to my question - in the fall of 1993, did not those on the Croat side, and for these purposes I'm including both Zagreb and the HVO Herceg-Bosna leadership, I'm including both when I say "the Croat side," isn't it true that during the fall of 1993 the Croat side saw, if you will, moving away from them, that the negotiations and political discussions at the time were moving away from anything allowing or setting up a Croat unit to something that ultimately became known as the Federation? That's the direction things were going in the fall of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, things were going towards the establishment of the Croat-Muslim federation in accordance with the Washington Agreement. That was the result of the political negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But before that fully happened, sir, isn't it correct that both Tudjman and Milosevic tried to get the idea of partition, if you will, back on track, that it was time to return to that concept that the real solution was a partition of Bosnia, and both Tudjman and Milosevic, in the second half of 1993, were once again calling for that position; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not witness that, and I don't know what to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't witness it, and I suspect you didn't witness a lot of things that Mr. Karnavas asked you about. I'm putting to you, as your state of knowledge and events, that was the case, wasn't it? You became aware, in the political dialogue that was going on in the second half of 1993 and as some of the concepts on the table, if you will, were changing, you knew, didn't you, surely, President Tudjman taking such a position, Slobodan Milosevic, that the idea was to return to a partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through speculations in the media, but I never did get a definite answer or position vis-a-vis this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's go to Exhibit P10700 in the third binder, P10700, a 2 November 1993 article by a news agency that Mr. President says is a highly reliable one, Agence France-Presse: "Zagreb, November 2, AFP: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman called Tuesday for resumption of the stalled Geneva peace talks on Bosnia-Herzegovina with the participation of Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Turkey and the United States." The fourth paragraph: "The Croatian leader's proposal amounted to a rejection of suggestions by international mediators Lord Owen and Thorvald Stoltenberg for a broader attempt to link all outstanding conflicts in the former Yugoslavia in a new global effort. "The Geneva talks, brokered by the United Nations and the European Community, and involving the warring Bosnian parties as well as leaders from Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro, broke down in September after the Muslim-led Bosnian parliament rejected proposals to divide the country into ethnic Croat, Muslim and Serbian mini-states. "Tudjman said the conference, broadened to include 'countries likely to effectively influence' the peace process, should keep the earlier partition proposal as its starting point." Now, you knew that's what was going on at the time; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to object, Your Honour. The first two paragraphs that were read, they are interpretations of whoever wrote this as to what was going on at the time. What they don't have are, for instance, the discussions that we saw in the presidential transcripts concerning Redman, the US's position of --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is commentary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well that's why --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I'm objecting, because right now the Prosecutor is pointing to two particular paragraphs that are the opinion of some unknown individual that I don't get to cross-examine here, I don't get to confront. This is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, all sides have used press articles exactly like I'm doing now, putting these questions to the witness, and what Mr. Karnavas has just done again is stand up and give the answer for the witness, who hasn't had a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's given his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's his commentary, his argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. You're right, Mr. Scott. Mr. Karnavas, you could have done that during the redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do what, Your Honour, do what? That's the problem. You allow these sorts of -- going off into this area, and then you limit me my time. It's not enough to say, "You can do -- spend as much time as you want on redirect," if I only have 95 hours when I'd asked for 150 and say, "Use it on redirect." Frankly, I don't see how it is that the Trial Chamber can just sit there when he's reading two paragraphs that are commentary. This is an analysis by somebody who wrote this article. How can he then say these are facts? That's my objection, the way he's trying to twist this article into believing that somehow this is Tudjman's position. Why not give all the information to the witness? That's my objection. And to say I can cover it on redirect, I need five or ten hours on redirect to cover everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you, and I'll just read it to you again - please listen to my question: "Tudjman said the conference broadened to include countries likely to effectively influence the peace process, should keep the earlier partition proposal at its starting point." Now, keep that in mind. A few moments ago I believe you agreed -- you ultimately did agree, after I asked you several times, that there was discussion around this time and it was being reported in the media that indeed Tudjman and Milosevic had taken this position. Now, that's correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He didn't agree to that. I object again. This is a mischaracterisation of the evidence. He never agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, can we go back a minute? Give me a moment, Your Honour, and I'll go back in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while he's at it, why not put something in front of the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you -- could you please moderate your tone a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. We need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's all to your credit that you're engaged, Mr. Karnavas, but the Chamber really doesn't need shouting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While we're looking for that:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Really, again, I've just quoted the language to you, I've read it to you now twice. You and others in the HVO leadership, the people that you met with practically every week at the government meeting, you were aware of President Tudjman and Milosevic indicating -- stating taking this position in the fall of 1993; correct? Whether you agree with this document or not, I put it to you, as Mr. Karnavas said, put something physical in front of you that might assist you, that might refresh your memory, whether you agree with it or not, can you tell these Judges you knew that was the position being put forward by Tudjman and Milosevic during this time period, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a little while ago, I learnt about that through the speculations in the media. That's where I read about it. I did not have any direct knowledge of that, any documents, any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, around this time the German government withdrawing its earlier support of the Tudjman government because, in fact, for the very reason that Tudjman had gotten too close to Milosevic on this issue?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you go, please, to Exhibit P10702. P10702.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to object to this sort of cross-examination. Where is something from the German government, something official? We're using the press now. This is a profound way of proving a case by an international organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Anything can be used as evidence, Your Honour. It can be a bloody shirt, it can be a piece of anything I've put in front of the witness, and the witness can clearly say. If he says he doesn't know or he doesn't agree, he can say so, and for that matter I don't have to put a single document in front of him; I can simply ask him the questions. So Mr. Karnavas is just dead wrong, and I wish he would stop being obstructionist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is another article by Agence France-Presse, and started on November 2nd, 1993, Zagreb, November 2nd, AFP: "Germany, one of Croatia's staunchest supporters in the Yugoslav conflict, can no longer 'identify' with Zagreb because of the latter's increasing alliance with Serbia, a German Deputy said here Tuesday," referring to a man named Hans Stercken. In the middle of the page: "Stercken, who arrived in Zagreb last Saturday for talks with top Croatian officials, also criticised Croatia President Franjo Tudjman for 'trusting too much' his Serbian counterpart Slobodan Milosevic." Now, do you remember around this time, sir, in November 1993, a very important -- a very important government that was generally supportive of Croatia withdrawing its support because of the Tudjman-Milosevic partition initiative? Surely you were reading the newspapers, surely you were watching television, surely you were participating in these government meetings.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was not in the government. And in the media that I was able to follow at the time, I could not find any statements to that effect. This document from the France Press Agency, well, this is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you keep saying you weren't in the government at this time. When did you stop being the head of the finance department of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established, I ceased being a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that didn't happen overnight, did it? It's just like we were talking about earlier today. It takes time to do these things, and the new government wasn't put in place until late November of 1993; isn't that the case? If you need to, we can go to presidential transcript, where President Tudjman picked the new government, if that will help you. You continued to be a member of the government until at least late November 1993, sir, and even after that, you were the deputy minister of finance, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I became the deputy minister of finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course I'm in the Chamber's hands, but I'm about to start a new topic and I do note that it's a couple of minutes before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have one hour fifteen minutes left when we resume tomorrow. Well, I have a fear because -- with all the objections. I was expecting you to finish now. If Mr. Karnavas requires four hours, well, the witness will have to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on the latitude that is being given to the Prosecution and the continuing -- the continuing observations by the Trial Chamber that I can just handle everything on redirect, at this point in time I'm making an oral application for additional time beyond that which has been allotted to me for my case. In other words, I'm asking for another 10 hours to be added to the 95 hours that I was given. I expect some consideration of this, because it would seem that the Trial Chamber is under the impression that I can handle all of these things on redirect, especially if we're going to be going into areas dealing with the implementation of the -- not just the Washington Agreement, but also the Dayton Peace Accords. I argued last week and I asked for a hearing at one point. We were promised a hearing. General Praljak indicated that a hearing was promised to us. We have yet to have that hearing. At what point -- where are the contours of this particular indictment? They keep growing over and over again. We are entitled to know what it is that we need to defend against, and now we have allowed the Prosecution to go into the implementation process of the Dayton Peace Accords. In other words, we now have to defend that process from 1995 all the way to 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Your request is in the transcript. It's 7.00 p.m. Witness, you'll return for the hearing tomorrow that will resume at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of November, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
